#8776. The 6 Best Folding Treadmills for Runners, Tested by a Treadmill Expert

We tested folding treadmills for running feel, size, storage, portability, speed, incline, and more to find the best models for every type of runner.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The best folding treadmills give you a real running experience without permanently eating up your floor space. I adore having a folding treadmill at home, because, living in a smaller space, I can easily stash it away or bring it out for a go. And this time of year, when there's sleet and snow? I don't want to miss out on a workout.

If you're like me and you want to be able to run a treadmill at home, but you can’t give away valuable space to a huge piece of fitness equipment? We get it. There’s a solution, though: A folding treadmill gives you the ability to pack up and store your ’mill between runs. Their compact size and light weight comes at a cost: They often don’t have as many convenient features we expect from a top-of-the-line model, nor do they offer huge inclines and top speeds. That said, most can do the basics effectively when you need them to, then fit in your closet when you’re done. The best folding treadmills, as we see them, offer a range of sizes and prices for casual runners and athletes in training.

The dream of shoving your treadmill under your bed between runs is alive in the Echelon Stride-6. This high-performance mill features a full-size, 20.5- by 60-inch running deck that can hit a max speed of 12.5 mph, but still manages to fold up tight. Personally, I store mine upright against a wall, sometimes hidden behind a curtain. It takes up about as much space as a few snowboards or a couple of winter coats. No, I'm not kidding, it's just that compact.

The Stride-6’s belt features low-response cushioning that creates a ride that feels closer to outdoor road running than treadmill running, which I love when I’m training for road races. Also, as an autistic sensory seeker, sometimes I really enjoy beating the hell out of the deck after a bad day. Are you also a sensory seeker, or have one in your life? If so, this is a solid choice. At full speed, with a 12 percent incline, this machine gives as good as it gets, too.

This treadmill does not have a touchscreen, though. Instead, it syncs directly to a running watch or tablet, for which it has an extra-large holder. The pre-loaded running programs are fine and dandy, but nothing to write home about. Echelon produces a paid workout video library like NordicTrack’s iFit, which you can access via an app, but it’s no different than any other virtual workout platforms without native support on the treadmill.

Let’s talk a little more about the folding mechanism, though, because that’s the reason to buy this treadmill. It is one of only a handful of options that doesn’t require any assembly. Unbox this beauty, unfold it, plug it in, and you’re good. It has an “autofold” feature that makes collapsing the treadmill feel seamless. All that you do is press the foot pedal, and the crossbar and board fold onto the surface of the treadmill. You can then store it flat on the ground or upright, which is a win for anyone who doesn’t have the permanent floor space available.

Also, after testing treadmill after treadmill in my house, I can confidently say my cats prefer the Stride-6, and I have no idea why. They're obsessed and I can't figure it out. It is also the easiest to store, fun to run on, and it's by far the easiest to move around.

When this treadmill is folded, it practically disappears. Fully folded, it drops to under 11 inches tall, which is easily flat enough to slide under a bed or stand upright in a closet corner. For anyone training for a marathon in an apartment, a spare bedroom, or a shared space, you know the value there. The SwiftFold mechanism handles it in one motion, and there’s no assembly required.

What I appreciate is that folding this flat usually means compromising on the machine underneath. This one doesn’t. You still get a dual brushless 4.0 HP motor, a 0–12 percent auto-incline, a 12.5 mph top speed, and a 300-lb weight capacity that matches most treadmills in its class. The 51.18 x 18.9-inch deck is a touch narrow for tall runners, and that is, admittedly an issue.But, when you add the real marathon course maps and an AI coach, along with that magical fold? At around $900 to $1,000 it’s a ‘mill that’s hard to say no to.

I will be the first to admit I was incredibly skeptical about this machine. I mean, it folds up to be smaller than your average card table. I have luggage that’s bigger than the G5i. But, I hear the cawing coming because I need to eat crow. It’s surprisingly stable and fun to run on. It’s really pretty smooth. It is more road-like than cushioned, so if you’re expecting pillowy surfaces, you’ll be disappointed. But if you’re worried you’re going to feel the fold seam, or feel super penned in, you won’t.

No, this is not a treadmill for tall runners. I’m 6-feet tall, and I’m at the tippy top end of the range of someone who should throw miles on this. But, that being said, if you’re shorter than I am, starved for space, and you want a folding treadmill with serious speed and incline, this is a fantastic option. One thing I will note, though: that first fold when you’re folding it isn’t as soft as you’d expect, and it’s kinda loud. But considering the fact that you could store it just about anywhere, and that it takes less than five minutes to set up and assemble? It’s freaking impressive as all get out. Like, truly wild territory, here.

If you’re looking for a serious running machine that also happens to fold, then you can’t do better than the NordicTrack Commercial 1750. Both Dengate and I really appreciated the feel of running on this machine, which has he called “Goldilocks” cushioning. The deck is firm enough that you don’t feel like you’re running on rubber but soft enough that it wasn’t as hard on our joints as a road run would be. We were also sold on the quick controls for both speed and incline changes, which are both easy to identify and toggle. I found that it stops a bit more abruptly than other NordicTracks: It’s not “knock you off your feet” fast, but there’s a little learning curve.

The Commercial 1750 has a large running surface, which I appreciate as someone who tends to wander on the ’mill a bit. All NordicTracks come with a trial subscription to iFit, the brand’s virtual workout library, which gives you dozens of programs, like marathon training companions, guided runs, and more. It costs extra after the first 30 days, but I think it’s a distinctive and worthwhile option if you like a guided workout. Of course, you can run on this treadmill without iFit, too.

On to the folding: The frame is huge–it weighs over 300 pounds–so it needs the hydraulic lift help that gets it to fold. The process could be a hair easier, but the balanced weight makes it fairly simple. Moving the 1750, on the other hand, is tricky. Sure, it technically has wheels so that you can roll it around, but that requires tipping the machine and balancing it while you do. Once you place it, you can fold it, but you’re better off leaving it where it is.

The Horizon 7.0AT was the easiest treadmill to get started and learn how to use, but its simplicity holds it back from being the outright best. It’s an old-school treadmill with no touchscreen display or video components, and that limits options for programming. That being said, it’s a very affordable option that gets the job done so long as you don’t need a guided workout or on-board entertainment.

The Horizon 7.0 does exactly what you expect and does a great job of it. It has a 20- by 60-inch running deck that’s plenty large enough for the majority of runners. I wish that it felt a little firmer underfoot, but other members of our team did not have the same complaint. The pre-loaded programs are easy to find if you know your way around a treadmill. (Most of the runners I spoke with are “set and forget” or running with program apps—which you can link through your watch or tablet—so it’s not a worry.) The toggles for speed and incline are intuitive and easy to use.

Folding this one is nice and easy, thanks to a hydraulic assist mechanism. Moving it around is pretty easy, too: The wheels line up in a better place than the 1750. It shrinks by nearly 40 percent when folded, which is genuinely impressive when you consider its massive build and huge incline range. One thing to keep in mind, though: That steep incline lifts you fairly high, so I do not recommend it for basement gyms unless you plan on running flat, or you live in a fancy place with 9-foot basement ceilings.

I’ve never met a treadmill that folds up smaller than the WalkingPad R2. In keeping with the brand, it’s made for walking, with a top speed of 3.7 mph and speed walking at 7.5 mph. And honestly? It’s so compact that you could reasonably put one of these in your home as a more portable complement to a standard, non-folding treadmill without feeling cramped. Use it as an under-desk treadmill or move it around to wherever you can find some free space.

It’s a fantastic treadmill for anyone who wants to get moving when they’d otherwise be sitting around. It features a smaller deck, super-responsive cushioning, and whisper-quiet motor. You could walk on it during a Zoom call with your microphone unmuted, and people would be hard-pressed to hear it. The cushioning means that you’re not going to wear yourself out while you work, and keeps you from bouncing around so badly that you can’t type.

One little thing I like about this folding treadmill is its smart “automatic mode,” which automatically detects your speed changes depending on where your feet are hitting the deck and adjusts as you go. That alone is worth the cost of the machine.

Folding this treadmill is a cinch, and so is storage, thanks to its low weight and small footprint. Even if you store it in a different room from where you use it, it’s only 55 pounds, so you can just haul it from space to space without any issue.

The team at Runner’s World has been testing all things running for decades. We work year-round on everything from shoes to treadmills. Personally, I have been running for over 20 years, running multiple marathons and ultras, and treadmill training is a huge part of my regimen. And I’ve been professionally reviewing products for nearly a decade.

Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate designed a rigorous testing protocol to measure a number of critical features in each and every treadmill that we test, and I wrote a specific rubric to test folding treadmills based on that protocol. This year alone, I have run on over 40 models, racking up almost 200 miles in the past several months. Dengate, who is “never not running,” has also put in miles on many of these models. With folding treadmills, there are several specific qualities we examine to separate the best from the just ok:

Having the ability to fold should not make a treadmill any less useful. While it’s impossible for them to maintain all of the features of certain non-folding treadmills, many or most of them are every bit as good. Some are so gozZod that they even appear on many of our guides.

Even with a compact folding model, it’s important to plan ahead and measure out the spaces where you plan to use and/or store your treadmill. Keep in mind that you need at least 2 feet of clearance surrounding your treadmill in every direction while you’re running. As someone who has put a Cat-shaped hole in the wall of her basement because I lost my footing, I cannot recommend this enough.

There’s a Right Way to Fold and a Wrong Way to Fold

This sounds like a no-brainer, but a folding treadmill should become more compact and easy to store when folded. There are a ton that technically have a folding mechanism but are not all that much smaller in their folded form. If the folded treadmill is too tall for a room, or if it doesn’t clear very much floor space, it doesn’t make sense.

A small running platform can prevent you from feeling comfortable at your full running stride, so we generally think that longer is better. (There are exceptions, of course: A walking pad doesn’t need a long belt.) Width is crucial for people with a wider stride or who tend to wander a bit, or those of us who run a bit duck-footed. A narrow belt can feel constricting when you’re running.

Don’t Worry Too Much About Max Speed and Incline

With folding treadmills especially, you only want as much power as you actually need. A faster max speed requires a bigger motor, which makes for a bigger, heavier treadmill. Most people will be just fine with 10 mph for running, and 3 or 4 mph for walking, so a huge motor isn’t necessary.

Inclines are controlled by a separate motor, so the same rule applies. Most of us don’t want to pretend we’re climbing Everest at the gym, so a 15 percent incline is overkill. It’s nice to have occasionally, but not a dealbreaker to go without.

What are some ways to stay safe on the treadmill while training?

With the treadmill setting the pace for you, it is important to select a pace that you feel capable of walking or running at, and use the safety equipment provided. Be sure you know where the automatic stop switch is and where the speed adjustment buttons are before starting to run/walk.

Should I adjust my mileage while using a treadmill?

Because treadmill running can be easier than road running, you may need to increase your mileage (or adjust speed and incline) when training on the treadmill to get the same level of workout you get from running outdoors. However, many people find treadmill running far less mentally stimulating, making it difficult to do longer distances indoors.

Is a treadmill a good way for newbie runners or walkers to start?

There are benefits of starting your training on a treadmill. The external pacing of the treadmill allows you to set a desired pace, then not have to think about maintaining it once it’s set. Treadmills are also indoors, which means inclement weather can’t stop you from running. They also can have screens attached, allowing you watch shows or follow a video workout instead of just listening to music. However, walking outdoors has been shown to be beneficial for mental health with the changes in scenery as you walk, increased vitamin D production from being in the sun, and decreased sensory stimulation with the absence of screens.

#8775. The 8 Best Running Gloves for Logging Cold-Weather Miles

Not feeling the tips of your fingers on a run is unacceptable—these gloves provide wind resistance and warmth.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 23, 2026: Several gloves on this list are on sale, including our Best Value, the Nike Pacer. Some pairs are low in stock, including the Ibex Kilometer Glove, which is only available in small. We will update accordingly as brands roll out their new winter inventory.

The first snowfall can be magical, but overcast skies and visible breath during a run can dampen the enthusiasm of any runner impatient for spring. To survive the everlasting cold, the trick is to layer properly so you don’t feel miserable during winter training. Stocking up on a winter running jacket, leggings, and pants is a no-brainer, but don’t forget to accessorize. I’m talking gloves here.

As a constantly cold person who has three sweatshirts piled onto the back of her office desk chair, I’ll never forget that one Santa 5-Miler when I left my gloves in my car. As I squeezed my hands into fists trying to retain warmth as I raced, I swore to never again run a winter race without full coverage over my five digits.

This winter has tested my cold-weather tolerance, dipping below zero degrees Fahrenheit more than once. But it’s a perfect breeding ground for glove—and mitten—testing. Here are my top picks.

I’ve worked at RW for eight years and started running XC in high school. I learned to embrace the cold this year, testing most of the gloves included on this list. I judged them by insulation, dexterity, and fit. I also had a little help from male staffers, who tested the men’s version of gloves—and became aghast learning that the women’s wasn’t similar.

Contributor Nick Hilden also provides tips on what to look for when shopping for gloves and answers your frequently asked questions on when to wear them, and on sizing and fit.

The Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Glove is included in our Best Winter Gear for Runners guide because it checks off all the boxes: double-knit insulation, reflective lining, windproof panels, and touchscreen-compatible fingertips. The stitching on the long cuffs ensures a secure, tailored fit around the wrists.

The Active Fleece kept my fingers warm for an hour during 32-degree and slightly below freezing runs. When the temperature dropped to 20, my fingers started to ache after a half hour in the cold.

My main critique is that they’re unisex sizing only. Even the smallest size, extra small, left some room above my fingertips, which made it difficult to grasp items I pocketed and zippers. The patch on the palm didn’t reach past my thumb and forefinger, which would have provided a soft area for nose wiping.

Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Glove Review

These gloves by the Swoosh are great for easing into cold weather. The sizing is sex-specific and true-to-size. They’re favorable for their sleek construction, making dexterity possible when you need to refuel midrun—or just grab your apartment key—and don’t want to remove your gloves.

Because of their thinness, your fingertips may start to ache once the thermometer hits below freezing. Still, they’re a great pair when you’re transitioning into colder weather or have a higher threshold to the cold.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

When you’re pitting gloves against mittens, it’s dexterity versus warmth. Gloves allow you to use your fingers, but mittens keep them together, thereby minimizing heat loss.

Even though I felt like I was running with oven mitts on my hands (the sizing is small/medium, medium/large), the Convertible Zip Mittens were great for braving workouts that dipped into the teens—and tens. The extra room also allows for doubling up if you really want to head out when it’s minus 1 degree Fahrenheit or less.

The Velcro tabs allow you to tighten the fit around the wrists, and the interior lining feels as plush as the felt on my very authentic Robin Hood hat from Nottingham.

If you’re prone to losing a mate when things come in pairs, TrailHeads sees you: a buckle guarantees your left and right mitt won’t be separated. Afraid of losing both mitts? Attach them to a carabiner on your duffel using the loops on the cuffs. The reflective zipper is a nice touch if you need to use your fingers midrun.

My one issue with the mittens: the material on the thumbs leaves snot trails.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

My coworkers thought I was heading out on the slopes or wearing garden gloves, but the Ibex Kilometer isn’t just for skiers (or gardeners). After a stretch of testing during a brief stay in New York City, the Kilometer gets my runner seal of approval. I tested them while logging runs in Central Park and the Hudson River Greenway, hitting gusts of wind on rolling hills and by the water. Temperatures varied from 20 to 40 degrees Fahrenheit; the Kilometer made my workouts more bearable.

The leather palms had excellent grip when I ran holding my phone, trying to find the best route back to my hotel. My fingers were shielded from the river’s wind chill and the ribbed cuffs kept my wrists toasty. But the biggest win for me was the soft, absorbent patch of fabric on each thumb. They were perfect for swiping my very runny nose when the wind speed was 15 mph.

If you run with your phone and whip it out a bunch of times midrun, these are your gloves; almost the entire palm is patterned with silicone grips. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible and sizing is sex-specific, which translates to no bunched fingers or agitation trying to scroll.

These gloves aren’t for extreme weather, but they’re great when things start to get nippy or when you’re heading out for a short winter run. However, there’s one thing TrailHeads must rectify: It’s a travesty that only the men’s version has a nose wipe patch. Why did they skimp on this feature with the women’s edition?

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

These aren’t the cotton gloves you wore in grade school. The Smartwool Liner offers so much more in terms of warmth and quality; it all starts with the woven material.

The fabric is merino wool, which regulates warmth, controls odors, and dries fast. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible, and you’re not limited to a small patch on the thumb when you need to wipe your nose (the glove itself is real estate). The ribbed cuffs fit snug, even on small wrists. They’re great to wear when the temperature is mid-30s; maybe even lower if you don’t have near-Raynaud’s hands like mine.

Despite coming in unisex with no extra-small option, I was surprised how well the small Vortex Gloves fit my hands and how easy it was to use my phone and text. The fleece layer feels soft on my skin and I’ll honestly never understand why a glove/mitt hybrid is so underrated. The mitten hood serves as wind protection; it’s great on gusty runs or when the temperature slowly rises. You can tuck in the entire hood above the wrist, with the hi-vis tape still partially showing.

The gloves aren’t for extreme cold, however. I ran in the Vortex Windblock when the temperature dipped in the teens and not even the mitt hood could stop my fingers from aching. That’s not the worst knock, since we’ve had abnormal weather below 10 degrees and most gloves on this list either didn’t make the cut or only lasted for half an hour before I had to ball my hands in the palms.

The Vortex Windblock also has snaps on the cuffs so you can store them attached.

Prone to losing your gloves? The snap on the lululemon Fast and Free prevents accidental separation and it’s just one standout reason you should buy this pair.

These sleek gloves have silicone grippers to keep you from dropping your phone midrun midtext, as well as “screen-conductive” finger pads that allow you to use your touchscreen.

Striking reflectivity details the back of the Fast and Free. That fabric is also soft enough to swipe your nose without causing the skin on your nostrils to peel.

Shop Men’s at shop.lululemon.com | Shop Women’s at lululemon.com

Winter runners should look for a pair of lightweight gloves that are warm enough to keep your hands cozy, but breathable enough to let air circulate. Look for technical fabrics—polyester and other synthetic materials are often your best bet for finding that balance.

Some blends are better than others though. In case of bad weather, it also makes sense to keep an eye out for a weather-resistant material that can protect against rain and snow, as well as cold, cutting winds. Moisture-wicking materials, such as merino wool, can also help deal with sweat and mitigate the impact of cold rain.

I also like when a glove fabric contains a small amount of a stretchy material, such as spandex or elastane, to ensure the gloves fit comfortably and snug. That said, skip the stretch if you like a glove that feels roomy inside.

On the other hand, I recommend avoiding heavy gloves made from nylon or polyurethane. These materials are often thicker, warmer and weatherproof, so they’re more likely to make you overheat. (Depending on the design, they may also make it hard to use your phone or check your smartwatch.)

Everyone has their own Goldilocks spot for how much warmth they need from their gloves. The important thing to keep in mind is that your body feels warmer while you’re running–speaking broadly, we recommend dressing for a run as if it's 10- to 20 degrees warmer than the temperature outside (including the wind chill.) That’s a good rubric for determining both when to start wearing gloves in the winter, and the level of protection you want against the cold.

Thinking about gloves specifically, your running gloves probably shouldn’t be as warm as your everyday winter gloves. A warmer glove will keep you going in colder temperatures but will cause you to sweat more, so it may not feel comfortable for long.

Winter nights come early, so visibility is an essential concern for all cold-weather running gear. If you frequently run near a road, or in areas with little street lighting, every item of clothing you wear, head to toe, should feature a reflective or high-visibility element.

In fact, gloves are among the most important pieces of reflective running gear you can wear. They catch drivers’ eyes especially well because your hands move as you run, creating a more noticeable effect.

When should I start wearing running gloves in the winter?

Every person feels differently about gloves, but as I said earlier in the piece, experts recommend dressing for a run as if it’s 10 degrees warmer than the effective temperature with the wind chill. If you normally wear gloves on a 50-degree day, start putting on gloves when it’s 40 degrees.

A good running glove should fit snug around your hand. If there’s room for your hand to move inside the glove, your skin may rub against the fabric and start to chafe. At the same time, it’s important to make sure they aren’t too tight, which might reduce circulation.

One way to check if you have the right fit is by doing a pinch test. Put on one glove, then pinch the fabric at the tip of a finger with your other hand. Ideally, you should have about a quarter inch of extra room.

Most glove brands use one of two measurements to determine sizing: The circumference of your fingers at the knuckles (without the thumb), and full hand length from the base of the hand to the tip of the middle finger. Check the product listing on the glove to see how the brand measures.

To measure the knuckle circumference, hold your fingers together, then wrap a measuring tape around your knuckles. Don’t squeeze your fingers too tight, though.

When measuring your full hand, make sure your middle finger is fully extended to ensure a proper measurement.

#8774. These Three Offseason Strength Exercises Can Help You Break Through Your Climbing Plateau

Build climbing strength this offseason with three simple moves for your upper body, legs, and core.

This time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time. If you’re thinking about winterizing your bike for the season, then it’s the perfect time to start looking at your strength training plan for the offseason.

For a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside. For others it takes form as time on fat bikes, skis, or even a pair of running shoes. Regardless of how your winter activities take shape, be sure to add some strength training to make sure you can hit your 2027 goals.

The workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training. Each exercise targets a different part of the body to dial in the strength you need when you are trying to power up climbs next year. The workout can be done as a stand-alone set of exercises or it can be added on to your current strength training plan.

So many cyclists want to just spend time in the saddle for training—that’s great up to a point. Eventually we all need to get off the bike and spend some time strength training to help break through those frustrating plateaus. These three overlooked exercises can help you elevate your climbs for 2027.

Today I had my first hill-focused ride after a few weeks focusing on running and trainer rides. The first steep pitch quickly reminded me how much I use my upper body while getting up a hill on the bike. As I climbed, I felt myself pulling on the handlebar with each pedal stroke while gravity was trying to pull me back. Developing the pull muscles is something that will benefit the whole kinetic chain while climbing. Bent-over rows in particular are a great upper-body exercise for this because they engage multiple muscle groups for one movement pattern. Rows can be done with so many different types of equipment: dumbbells, kettlebells, TRX Suspension Systems, elastic bands, and more. Here’s how I recommend doing them with dumbbells.

One of the reasons I love deadlifts for cyclists is because they are exercises that works almost all the muscles through the kinetic chain in one simple move. As we climb, we are pulling energy through our upper body, driving through the hips, and pushing the power through our legs into the pedals. This exercise trains the muscles through your arms, back, and core, while simultaneously working the muscles throughout your legs. Another reason deadlifts are one of my go-to exercises is that they can be done with several different types of equipment. My favorite equipment for this exercise is a barbell, but deadlifts can be done with dumbbells and kettlebells too.

Recovery Tip: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is very real, and depending on the person, your muscle burn can last for a few days after your training session. Plan accordingly for your rides following a heavy weight day. Listen to your body and add a recovery ride or off-bike activity if that's what you need.

Your core is what ties everything in your body together, so it is integral to grow your stability and power here. While riding today, I was trying to really be in tune with how I was using my core when climbing. When I was in the saddle I felt like the focus from my core was on stability, allowing for a sound upper body while pushing power through my legs and out of the pedals. My simple go-to core exercise to improve climbing is a plank with cross-body knee taps. This works stability through your core while working the internal obliques through the cross-body motion of the knee tuck. This exercise will really show its gains when you get out of the saddle as the climb pitches up.

A quick note on consistency: strength training will give you the best results when you incorporate it in your plan week after week. It will offer significantly diminished results if you are sprinkling it in sporadically. If you are able to, try to commit to adding strength training consistently for a four- to six-week block and see how that impacts your rides.

Our strength training program can help get you started with a more in-depth workout plan. It’s important to remember it does not matter where you are in your cycling journey, there are gains to be found from adding some level of strength training to your calendar.

#8773. After a Decade of Refusing to Use a Treadmill, I Finally Gave In. Here’s How It’s Making Me a Better Runner.

Cold, dark days don’t have to derail your running. The treadmill might be the fix you need.

When the weather dipped below freezing for the first time last winter and the sun began to set at 4:30 p.m., I knew I’d have to leave my typical after-work miles behind. Cold weather and early darkness have always been an easy one-two punch to my running motivation.

I’d also long held another line in the sand: I didn’t run on treadmills—at least not since high school gym class. I took to calling myself a “purist” because I didn’t think running was worth it if it wasn’t outside in nature. I believed my cause was noble, but really, I was just piling up excuses not to run in the winter.

So I decided to give treadmill running a chance. I set out to complete one to two easy runs per week for a month to see if it could help me stay consistent through the winter. Within a few weeks, I was running more than I ever had in winters past—and reconsidering what held me back all those years.

My experiment started after work in late fall. I turned to one of the Bowflex treadmills we have at Runner’s World headquarters. Earlier in the day, my editor casually mentioned that my Apple Watch would sync directly to the treadmill for a more accurate reading, a suggestion that made me more excited to get started on my test.

I walked up to the treadmill and the first thing I noticed was that if I wanted to, I could put my Netflix password into the built-in monitor and fire up an episode of Brooklyn Nine-Nine for the 200th time. While this capability isn’t very advanced as far as treadmill features go nowadays, the shift from the bare-bones experience I remembered from a decade ago in high school gym class amazed me.

I decided to go simple for my first run, tapping in with my Apple Watch and committing to a 30-minute easy effort with just a podcast to entertain me.

The run itself was good, but left me puzzled. I immediately focused on how each foot strike offered a different sensation than I was used to outside. After a minute of adjusting the belt speed, I settled into a pace that felt similar to my outdoor easy runs. What I found, though, was that the treadmill speed read a completely different pace than my outdoor runs.

After 30 minutes at zero incline, I completed just 2.56 miles at an 11:51 pace with my heart rate right at my usual 150 beats per minute (bpm). That 11:51 average was nearly two minutes slower than my outdoor 10:00 easy pace, but I felt like I was right at my normal outdoor effort level.

Still, I walked away encouraged. I logged a run, avoided the weather, and felt great doing it.

My experiment continued with more 30-minute easy runs over the next couple of weeks. Each one raised the same question: Why did an effort that felt identical to my normal 10:00 outdoor easy runs translate to a treadmill pace of well over 11:00 per mile? Adding to the confusion, I got a new watch (the Coros Pace 4), and it consistently recorded slightly longer distances than the treadmill itself displayed.

After my third run, I brought all my questions to a chat with Birmingham-based RRCA level II- and USATF-certified run coach Alex Morrow, founder of Resolute Running. I described to him how, on the treadmill, I felt I was giving a similar effort compared with my outdoor runs, but was running at a significantly slower pace, and I asked him why he thought this was the case.

“When you’re outside and you’re running at an easy pace, you’re looking at the trees, you’re waving at other runners, and your mind gets to dissociate from what you’re doing,” Morrow says. “When you’re on a treadmill, there’s very little stimulation,” beyond your body moving.

Because I’d been running exclusively outdoors since high school, I was used to looking around at the cars as they passed by, the birds in the air, and any number of distractions along my route. As soon as I hopped on the treadmill, though, none of that was there to capture my attention. Right away, I locked in on the difference in every step, and became consumed by how far off my pace ended up being from what I expected.

Changing a long-held belief is tough, especially when it’s rooted in identity. “It’s like turning a battleship around,” says Morrow. “It takes time and it’s never easy.” In my case, the belief that “real runners” don’t use treadmills stuck around for years.

Once I started running on one, though, I accepted it as a suitable tool for consistent running almost immediately. The hardest part of flipping my mindset wasn’t logging the miles or dealing with boredom, it was simply stepping onto the belt in the first place.

If you’re new to treadmill running, or have avoided it for the same reasons I did, my best advice is to try it with an open mind. Don’t worry if your pace looks slower than what you’re used to seeing outside. That mental hurdle of mine ended up not really mattering much. I let effort guide my runs, my podcasts entertain me, and I judge my success based on time on feet rather than actual miles.

My biggest takeaway from the experience was consistency. According to Morrow, that’s where treadmill running becomes one of the most powerful tools a runner can use, especially in the winter.

Through my trial efforts, I realized I wasn’t frustrated with the treadmill itself, I was simply focused on learning more about my running. Curiosity helped me keep a steady schedule, and in just a few weeks, I’d already run more in the winter than I had in years.

“Consistency is so much more important than having one killer workout,” Morrow explains. “I would much rather you have four or five average workouts than three killer workouts.” This idea counters how a lot of runners think about training, especially when motivation dips. It’s flashy to chase breakthrough days in perfect conditions, but you build fitness by stacking days together, even when the circumstances aren’t ideal.

For runners who live in areas heavily impacted by harsh winter weather, the treadmill is a saving grace. “Something is always better than nothing,” Morrow says. “Jogging three miles on a treadmill is better than skipping your workout completely because it’s cold outside.”

When weather threatens to derail a week of training, the opportunity that a treadmill provides becomes crucial to your development as a runner. “Consistency creates physiological adaptations in your body that allow you to reach your goals,” Morrow says. Those adaptations include a boost in aerobic fitness development, running economy, VO2 max, and lactate threshold, he continues. It’s adaptations like these that establish an excellent fitness base for marathon training.

Looking back on my career as a recreational runner, my biggest mistake wasn’t refusing to run on the treadmill; it was letting that ignorance cost me months of consistent running every year. Now, the excuses that held me back are gone. I’ve continued using the treadmill to not only knock out frequent easy runs but conquer the occasional interval workout or speed session.

#8772. Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

A quick check can reveal whether your saddle height is working against you.

A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours. It can show up as pain behind the knee, pressure in the saddle, numbness, or that familiar feeling that you’re reaching for the pedal instead of driving through it.

And because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix. Riders often blame the saddle itself, their bib shorts, or even their flexibility when the issue is simply that the seat is a little too high.

To get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change. Check out Bicycling’s Guide to the Perfect Bike Fit.

That said, saddle height is also where fit advice gets messy. There isn’t one perfect number that works for everyone, and the usual rules of thumb are only starting points. Your ideal height depends on your body, your mobility, your injury history, your cleat setup, and more.

Quick Signs Your Saddle May Be Too High• Pain behind the knee • Saddle sores or numbness • Discomfort where your hamstrings meet your glutes • Rocking hips while pedaling • Reaching for the pedal at the bottom of the stroke Quick Fix• Lower the saddle a few millimeters, do a real ride, and reassess.

Here’s how to tell whether your saddle may be too high and a simple at-home check you can do before your next ride.

Saddle height is one of the first things riders adjust, and for good reason. When it’s close, you feel smoother and more comfortable. When it’s off, the problems can spread everywhere.

But this is where people get tripped up: saddle height is important, but it is only one element in an interconnected system. If your cleats are in the wrong place, your saddle is too far forward or back, or your crankarms don’t suit you, changing saddle height alone may not solve much. It’s the beginning of fit, not the whole thing.

A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel. Two riders with the same height and inseam may still end up at different saddle heights because bodies aren’t identical and neither are pedaling styles.

Pain is the clearest warning that something in your position needs attention. Riding is hard. Suffering through an interval is one thing. Pain caused by pressure, strain, or repeated irritation from a bad setup is another.

A saddle that’s too high often shows up in a few predictable ways:

This is the classic one. If you feel pain at the back of the knee, especially after longer rides or harder efforts, a too-high saddle is one possible cause.

But not the only one. Fit problems tend to overlap. So treat this as a clue, not a verdict.

If the back of your pedal stroke feels strained, tight, or tuggy, especially when you’re trying to make power, your saddle may be a little high.+.

A high saddle can make you unstable on the bike. Instead of sitting planted, you start shifting and searching. That extra motion can increase friction and pressure, which can mean hot spots, sores, and numbness.

If your hips are dropping side to side at the bottom of the pedal stroke, there’s a decent chance you’re compensating for too much saddle height.

Some riders point their toes naturally. But if you’re really reaching at the bottom of the stroke and compensating by going toes-down, that can be another sign the saddle is too high.

Rocking hips can also happen with a saddle that’s too low. So can a toes-down pedaling style. Tight hamstrings, limited mobility, weak core stability, and other fit issues can all muddy the picture. Back-of-knee pain can come from saddle height, but it can also come from saddle fore-aft, cleat setup, or a combination of things.

That doesn’t make the signs worthless. It just means you should think in patterns, not absolutes.

If you have knee pain plus hip rocking plus pressure and instability in the saddle, now the case gets stronger.

Todd Carver, Specialized’s human performance manager, shared a simple check that can help flag a saddle that may be too high.

If the distance from heel to pedal is more than about one centimeter, your saddle could be too high.

The result is a prompt to look closer, not a green light to make significant changes without further investigation.

Don’t make a giant change. That’s how you turn one problem into several problems.

Start small. Lower the saddle a few millimeters at a time, then ride it long enough to notice whether the change actually helps. One short spin around the block is not enough. You want enough ride time to see whether the pain eases, whether your pedaling feels smoother, and whether you stop shifting around on the saddle.

If you’re dealing with persistent pain, don’t keep self-diagnosing forever.

A good fit pro can sort out whether saddle height is the actual problem or just the most obvious symptom.

Riders fixate on saddle height because it feels fundamental. And it is. But it’s also just one part of a system.

A high saddle can absolutely cause trouble. So can cleat position. So can saddle setback. So can crank length. So can your mobility. The goal is not to chase some magic formula you found online. It’s to get to a position that lets you pedal smoothly, make power comfortably, and finish rides feeling worked, not damaged.

That’s why the best takeaway is a modest one: use the common signs, do a quick check, make small changes, and listen to what your body tells you.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. #8771. Like Jess McClain, I Took Time Off From Running—and Came Back Stronger. These Signs Mean It’s Time to Step Away.

Plus, the benefits you’ll gain from a break.

They say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running. But by “distance,” I don’t mean bumping up my mileage or running farther. I mean taking time and space away from my sport during seasons when I feel burned out, lost, or simply exhausted.

Around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch. The second I crossed the finish line, all I wanted to do was let my running shoes collect dust, avoid my local trail, and avoid stepping foot in the gym for a while.

Professional distance runner and New York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago. At that time, she consistently stopped hitting her paces in her workouts and decided to step back from running—a break that lasted about two years.

In my case, I wasn’t as decisive. For months, I resisted the idea that I needed to take a break.

I’d heard that a month is generally how long you need to recover from a marathon, so I told myself that’s when I would jump into winter base training. But every time I tried to get back out there, I got bored and I struggled to recover from my runs. I waited until summer for the urge to work out again, but it never really came back.

For a while, I felt like getting burned out was my fault, that I must have pushed too hard in training. Looking back now—and with help from an expert—I understand that my break was exactly what I needed to get back to my sport in a sustainable way.

My break from running lasted about nine months, and I came back feeling like the runner I had always been before. Plus, I raced one of my fastest half marathons as my comeback.

Below I offer the telltale signs it’s time for a break from running, what a “break” really means, and the benefits you can gain from stepping away from the sport for a while—even if it seems impossible to do so at first.

The farther away I got from my training cycle, the more I realized how much I overtrained. I’d been strength training for 90 minutes three times a week with heavy weights while balancing 30-plus-mile weeks and 20-mile long runs. As I gained more perspective after my race ended, I noticed signs that I was in desperate need of a break.

“Pay attention to trends and patterns [throughout your training],” Erin Ayala, PhD, a sports psychologist, certified mental performance consultant, and founder of Skadi Sport Psychology, tells Runner’s World. “We all have bad days where the numbers aren’t coming together or a run feels harder than it normally does at a given pace. But if it continues to occur, then it can definitely be a sign to take a break,” she says.

Ayala says there are three main factors that often lead to athletic burnout. Here’s what each can look like, and how I experienced them.

You might need to take a step back if you find yourself hitting training plateaus despite putting in your best efforts.

I picked a training plan that included paces far too fast for my fitness level at the time, so every interval workout I did felt difficult, and my paces never really improved. The longer the intervals got, the farther I was from my desired split. But I kept checking off the weekly workouts anyway.

This lack of personal achievement and growth can halt your motivation levels. “When you’re not able to progress and you lose sight of [personal achievements] you’re just going through the motions, that’s a really big red flag,” Ayala says.

After the first month or so, marathon training started to feel more like a chore and I felt really tired and disconnected during my workouts. I figured it was probably normal because I had never run a marathon before, but it turns out that’s not how you should expect to feel daily in your training. “If the workouts are just a grind and you’re having to peel yourself off of the couch in order to get them in, and that’s a sustained pattern, then that’s another big red flag,” Ayala says.

A change in my relationship with running and my “why” meant grappling with my identity as a runner, which Ayala says is the third factor that can contribute to athletic burnout. You might ask yourself questions like, “Why do I even do this anymore?” and “What’s the point?” She says that if those questions linger for more than a week or so, then that’s a sign you might need a break.

By the time I got to the start line, I questioned why I was even there, and all I could do was get through it. “There’s a very real sense of grief and loss, and that’s really scary,” when taking a step back from running, Ayala explains. “Often we hang on quite desperately to our athletic identity when it’s also okay to move on and to do something different.”

Once I knew I needed a break from running, I didn’t quite know how to hit pause.

Then Ayala pointed out that perfectionism can affect your relationship with your sport. And simply hearing that helped me realize why I needed to step away.

There are two types of perfectionists, Ayala explains. The first type is the high achiever, who wants to be the best and perform at the top as much as possible. The second type of perfectionist takes a more “maladaptive form.” These individuals are highly motivated by others’ perceptions and expectations, she says. They might fear failure and generally don’t want to disappoint people.

That second type of perfectionism resonated with me because I realized I was listening to a nagging voice in my head that expected me to give absolutely everything I had to my training. And if I didn’t, I would face that critical voice’s judgment and let it fill me with disappointment and shame.

“Breaks can be helpful because they essentially force you to turn that perfectionistic tendency off. They’re a good way to keep yourself balanced,” Ayala adds.

Once I knew this and decided to take a break, I figured out how to fill my time.

Those first few months after marathon training, I was so excited to not think about running at all. Instead, I looked forward to filling my free time by rebooting my old Webkinz account (an online virtual-pet game popular in the mid-2000s), decorating my new apartment, and watching a lot of TV.

“First, just give yourself time. Then, you can create other bite-sized goals like daily movement, getting outside, spending time with friends, or exploring different hobbies,” Ayala suggests.

When I passed the two-month mark of my break, I took up pottery classes. While that hobby didn’t last, it gave me the space I needed from running.

I knew, deep down, that rest was probably what I needed. But when I took time off, I felt too anxious and ashamed to even enjoy it: I kept thinking about how much time I was wasting and how out-of-shape I felt. “The problem [with athletic burnout] isn’t that you just need to motivate yourself harder. You need to rest in order to get that intrinsic motivation back,” Ayala says.

Ayala explains that if we lose our intrinsic motivation, we often rely on feelings of shame and discipline to keep up with our routine, which ultimately isn’t sustainable.

When I was honest with myself, I found my new “why” for running—my intrinsic motivator—and that was because of how strong, creative, and capable it makes me feel.

One piece of advice from Ayala especially resonates with me: Accept where you’re at and normalize taking a break. “I would argue that getting burned out is a very normal and expected part of being an athlete,” she says. “If you are an athlete long enough, you are going to get burned out at some point and that’s okay. It doesn’t mean that you’re doing something wrong.”

Once I accepted that I was dealing with a longer-term case of burnout and some depression, I began to see light at the end of the tunnel. I set bite-sized goals, per Ayala’s suggestion, and began by committing to running just five minutes a day for a month. With that, running clicked for me again.

Looking back on my time away from running, I don’t view it with shame or anxiety anymore. I see it as both a period of my life when I learned about myself as an athlete and about how my brain works. It was also a time of physiological and mental recovery from so much training stress.

By stepping away, I unlocked a new life experience that can help inform me if—and probably when—I experience burnout again. That perspective shift alone lifts so much weight off my shoulders.

Plus, I’ve come back to the sport now feeling refreshed. I ran one of my fastest half marathons and feel ready to tackle another training plan. I have the drive to set and achieve goals again. And that’s an irreplaceable benefit to taking some time away.

#8770. Best Cheap Exercise Bikes That Feel Surprisingly Expensive

Light on price, heavy on performance—these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best ride for your money.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

There are plenty of reasons to start riding inside. Questionable weather, overly packed schedules, and less daylight can cause outdoor riders to head inside for some indoor saddle time. It’s also possible you’re someone who doesn’t ride outside and you just want a good low-impact workout in the comfort of your own home—without breaking the bank.

Recently we did extensive testing in the office on different exercise bikes. I found that some people who don’t ride bikes outside may actually prefer some of the less expensive exercise bike options. Some of the higher-end exercise bikes we tested feel like a real bike outside—and pair with specific apps like Zwift for when you want to get some group rides or racing in. If you aren’t used to a bike outside, then getting comfortable in that position can be a hard transition. More narrow saddles, a more aggressive position, and controls that simulate the shifters on a bike may not be what you want. Largely, these more inexpensive exercise bikes have more upright positions, wider and more padded saddles, and controls that would resemble the exercise bike you might see on the floor of a fitness center.

Keep in mind that inexpensive is relative—the bikes we have on this list range from about $200 up to $700. If you’re looking to boost your mood, stay consistent, or supplement your training with an affordable indoor cycling bike, these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best mix of value, performance, and reliability.

If you're further along in your indoor training journey and none of the bikes on this list feel like the right fit, take a look at our reviews of the Peloton, Zwift Ride V2, and other premium models.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike operates a 35-pound flywheel that provides a smooth and quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable via a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately, if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches, and allows riders to adjust the handlebar height as well as the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Using the single-button monitor, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned as you exercise. Just below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame is designed to provide stability and durability, but it's easy to move if you tip it up onto the small wheels on the front edge.

Besides being designed to look like an entry-level Peloton, the Yesoul S3’s biggest selling point is its Bluetooth connectivity, which pairs with the Yesoul Sports App (on both iOS and Android) and works with Zwift and other interactive training apps. All your workout data, including distance, time, calories burned, speed, heart rate, odometer, and cadence, is tracked and easy to access.

The bike has a quiet belt drive and magnetic resistance, with 100 levels that are easy to adjust with a knob. With a height- and distance-adjustable seat and handlebar, the S3 is built to fit riders from 4-feet-9-inches to 6-feet-2-inches—though riders at the higher end of that range and those with disproportionately longer legs might find the riding position to feel a bit “off.” The bike is easy to move on two small transport wheels, and it comes in both white and black models for a sleek, Peloton-like aesthetic.

This is a fantastic price for a budget bike that delivers a Peloton-like experience. It has the same sleek silhouette, with a saddle that adjusts both up/down and fore/aft, plus an adjustable handlebar height—just like the real thing. The belt-drive system is another big plus, keeping noise to a minimum so the only sounds you hear are your own effort (and hopefully some music to cover it up).

To keep costs down, this bike skips the large built-in display, instead offering a tablet holder and Bluetooth connectivity. That means you can ride with any third-party app you prefer—including Peloton classes—using your own device. At this price, it’s a fair trade-off. But if you want a built-in screen, Merach offers a similar model with that feature for about $450 more

Merach’s newest bike, the A26 Aura, is one of the best Peloton competitors I’ve seen. It follows the familiar design cues of premium exercise bikes — a sturdy frame, heavy flywheel, and whisper-quiet belt-drive system. The seat adjusts up and down as well as fore and aft, and the handlebar also moves vertically for a comfortable fit.

At its current sale price, the Merach A26 Aura makes a compelling case as one of the best values on this list.

The Echelon Connect Sport 2 delivers a Peloton-like experience at a more affordable price. It connects via Bluetooth to the Echelon Fit app, allowing you to track speed, distance, and calories. If you’re taking a live class, you can also view your ranking on the leaderboard. The app offers over 40 live classes daily and a library of more than 15,000 on-demand sessions. While the bike doesn’t have a built-in screen, its device holder accommodates tablets up to 8 inches wide.

That said, you don’t need the connected features to get a great workout. At its core, this is a solid, well-built exercise bike with a heavy flywheel and 32 resistance levels, manually adjusted with a knob behind the handlebar. The bike features a “one size fits most” design, with adjustable saddle and handlebar positions to suit most adults. However, some shorter riders have reported difficulty positioning the saddle close enough to the handlebars for a comfortable fit.

With Bluetooth and USB connectivity to the Schwinn ConnectTM, Zwift, and MyFitnessPal apps, this stationary bike is a great option for interactive workouts—particularly if you want to work through pre-programmed sessions and track your progress over time. The bike has the standard DualTrack console shared by similar-level Schwinn and Nautilus products, which has two sharp, backlit LCD screens loaded with 29 workouts.

Unlike many of the bikes we've selected that adjust gradually in difficulty at the turn of a knob, this model has 25 preset levels of magnetic resistance, which provides a nice range in difficulty. The seat and handlebar adjust by height and angle to fit users from 4-feet-6-inches to 6-feet-6-inches; however, as always, those at the far ends of the range might have more difficulty getting a comfortable fit. Ultimately, the bike is a solid package for the price—especially if you can catch one on sale for around $400.

Looking for a cheap home exercise bike that will neither take over your space nor break the bank? When not in use, this compact device folds down to half its size and can be easily rolled into a closet or tucked under a bed.

While it may have a minimalist design, it still has the basic functionality needed for a workout. It touts 12 levels of magnetic resistance, adjusted via a knob below the handlebar, that allows you to adjust the intensity as needed. The built-in LCD screen, although very basic, keeps track of key workout stats, including distance, time, speed, calories burned, and heart rate.

Users love how quiet this bike is, making it perfect for multitasking or watching TV while riding. Though it may not provide the high resistance some hardcore riders seek, many praise it as a “sturdy, well-built machine” with a “comfortable seat and great height adjustability.”

Just like with a regular bicycle, if you want the best experience on your indoor bike, it’s important to get the proper fit. Josh Taylor, a global brand ambassador for the online fitness site Spinning, recommends finding an indoor cycling bike that puts you in the same position as the bike you’re accustomed to riding outside.

For example, if your daily rider is a road bike, look for an indoor cycling bike with a handlebar option that incorporates a traditional bullhorn bar and mimics the hand-position options of drops and brake hoods. However, if you’re already used to taking studio classes, an indoor cycling bike with just the traditional bullhorn-style bar will work great, says Ben Sharp, three-time Order of Ikkos medal recipient and founder of Sharp Coaching.

If you don’t ride at all outside or in a spin class yet, then it will take a bit more playing around with the exercise bike to figure out sizing and position. Start with getting saddle height set up correctly, then if you can adjust reach to the handlebars that’s step two. For the reach shoot to have a slight bend in the elbows and remember to keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. Matt Phillips, Senior Test Editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on dialing in saddle height. What applies to saddle height on an outdoor bike largely applies to exercise bikes as well. “A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel,” says Phillips.

Join Bicycling All Access for more in-depth gear reviews

When you’re riding an outdoor bike, you’re mostly working against inertia as you pedal. In order to recreate that sensation and effort on a stationary bike, manufacturers have to simulate that resistance in some way. Most choose to use a fan or a flywheel (a weighted disc that spins as you pedal).

Flywheels work by storing inertia as they spin, and smoothing out the pedal stroke to eliminate that choppy up and down motion you’d otherwise experience. For most budget spin bikes, a heavier flywheel means a smoother ride, though some bikes opt for a light (8-pound) flywheel that maintains its inertia by spinning four times as fast instead.

Since the pedals on spin bikes are fixed to the flywheel (no coasting), the smooth-moving mechanism helps keep your pedaling consistent. These bikes will usually have a knob or lever that allows you to adjust the resistance, making it harder or easier to pedal, independent of your cadence (how fast you’re spinning the pedals). If you’re used to riding a bike outside, then think about it like riding a fixed-gear bike or fixie.

Fan-operated resistance bikes are a bit simpler: As you pedal, the fan blades push against the air around the machine. Your cadence is directly related to the amount of effort required to push the pedals, meaning these bikes don’t allow you to spin at a fast cadence with low resistance, which can be nice for warming up or cooling down.
