#8763. The World’s Hardest Beer Run? This Brutal Race Sends Runners Up a Mountain—With a Keg of Beer on Their Back

Runners carry as much as 130 pounds, including full kegs of beer, through a Slovakian mountain range.

Running up a rocky and technical trail more than a mile above sea level is tricky enough. Imagine doing it with a keg of beer strapped to your back—because this is exactly what competitors in the Sherpa Rallye, held on October 24, had to contend with.

Male entrants in the race shoulder a traditional wooden carrying frame, which resembles a sled but is loaded high with a 30-liter (about 8 gallons) keg of beer, plus other supplies (including large bottles of water) that add up to more than 130 pounds (60 kg). Women commonly carry cases of beer and materials that make their load weigh about 44 pounds (20 kg).

Since 1985, this unique annual race has been taking place on the unforgiving flanks of the High Tatras mountains in Slovakia. It starts just above the town of Starý Smokovec and finishes at Zbojnícka chata, a mountain refuge perched like an alpine eyrie 3.5 miles up the steep and rough track.

The High Tatras are home to Europe’s last remaining group of old-school mountain porters, many of whom take part in the race, which was started by a porter named Viktor Beránek to help bring workers together. They are locally and colloquially known as horský šerpa (mountain sherpas)—although they have no connection to the Sherpas of the Tibetan Himalaya, a distinct ethnic group, and are more correctly called horský nosi (mountain carriers).

However you refer to them, each season they manually transport heavy supplies to the mountain huts, refuges, and chalets that hikers use for shelter while trekking the local trails. And herein lies the rub, because once the Sherpa Rallye runners reach Zbojnícka chata, they don’t even get to celebrate by supping the goods they have just transported up to the hut—it goes in the stores for use over winter.

#8762. The One Piece of Cold-Weather Gear I Never Leave at Home

It’s cheap, packable, and useful enough that I bring it even when the forecast looks mild.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

From 55 degrees down to 25, I bring one piece of cold-weather gear on every ride: a neck buff. It isn’t the most exciting item in my kit, and it won’t make a dramatic difference in a gear photo. But it’s useful across a wider range of temperatures than almost anything else I own, and it costs far less than most winter gear cyclists spend serious money on.

At 55 degrees, I can wear it loosely around my neck and cut the wind without feeling bundled up. As the temperature drops, that little bit of insulation becomes more valuable. Covering your neck makes you feel warmer, and the buff also helps close the gap at the top of your jacket. Cold air sneaking in around the collar can make an otherwise reasonable layering setup feel inadequate. A buff helps keep that draft out.

When it gets really cold, I pull it up over my ears and face. It’s a simple way to add coverage without committing to a heavier balaclava for the whole ride. And if the temperature changes, or I start working harder on a climb, I can pull it back down in a few seconds. It takes up almost no space in a jersey pocket, which means there’s little reason to leave it at home.

Neck buffs grew out of a practical problem familiar to motorcycle riders: keeping cold, wind, and road dust off your neck and face. Riders already used bandanas and other neck cloths; the stretchy tube made that protection easier to wear under a helmet. Skiers adopted it too, which may be why people associate it with snow sports.

There is no shortage of expensive cycling accessories that promise to keep you warm while riding. Many are quite good. But few come close to the humble neck buff in terms of how practical, simple, and cheap it is. It’s an adaptable piece of kit that’s just as useful on a cool ride that doesn’t quite call for full winter kit as it is on a truly cold ride, when every gap and exposed bit of skin becomes a problem. It’s a small thing, which is exactly why I never leave home without it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#8761. This Is the Minimum Amount of Strength You Need in the Offseason to Get Ready for Your Next Training Block

Scale back your running between races while using your time in the weight room to build a stronger foundation.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

After months of long runs and tough workouts, you’ve finally crossed the finish line of your goal race. Now, it’s time to recover—and figure out what’s next.

While you can scale back your running in the offseason, it’s worth making room for strength training. Even a short time in the weight room can help you build a stronger foundation for your next training block.

The good news? You don’t need to spend all your newfound free time in the gym to make progress. By hitting the following minimum amount of strength work each week, you set yourself up to handle more mileage and run more efficiently when it’s time to chase a new goal.

In the first two weeks after your race, you should focus mainly on rest and getting back into easy jogging. After that, aim to add at least two strength sessions per week to your routine, exercise physiologist Heather Milton, C.S.C.S., previously told Runner’s World. Milton says these offseason strength sessions should focus on heavier weights (just make sure you work up in weight!) and a low-to-moderate number of reps.

During these heavy lifting workouts, athletes should aim to complete four to six sets of one to five reps of each exercise, pausing for two to four minutes in between each set, strength coach and physical therapist Lisbeth Hoyt, D.P.T., C.S.C.S., previously told Runner’s World.

While running is your main focus during marathon training (or any race distance, for that matter), strength sessions often help you maintain the strength you already have, Milton explains. But between training blocks, you can put more emphasis on building strength.

“Plus, when you start training for your next marathon, you’ll be in a stronger position to increase your running volume again because you’ve strengthened all of the areas of your body that were impacted by your previous race, which can help prevent injuries,” Milton adds.

You might associate heavy lifting with short sprinters or football players—athletes who focus on quick, explosive movement, rather than steady endurance. But building stronger muscles through heavy lifting supports long-distance running, too.

For starters, lifting heavier weights helps you build muscular strength, which translates to improved running economy, New York City-based strength and run coach Yusuf Jeffers previously told Runner’s World. Meaning, heavy lifting can help you use less energy to run at a given pace.

Research backs this up. A review published in Sports Medicine in 2023 examined several types of strength training in middle- and long-distance runners, including lifting heavy, submaximal lifting, isometric exercises, and plyometrics. The researchers found that lifting high loads—at least 80 percent of a person’s one-rep max—had the greatest effect on improving running economy at faster speeds. (Plyometrics worked particularly well for improving economy at slower speeds.)

The benefits extend beyond your muscles, too. Hoyt explains that strength training can support connective tissues and bone health.

It’s important to remember lifting “heavy” looks different for everyone. If you’re new to strength training or you’re unfamiliar with a particular movement, start by learning proper form and gradually work up in weight, Hoyt says.

Hoyt suggests focusing on movements such as squats, deadlifts, lunges, and rows, encouraging athletes to move slowly and with control.

#8760. Second Air Force National Signing Day Held at U.S. Capitol

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

When an American joins any branch of the United States military, they repeat an Oath of Enlistment to make the commitment official.

I do solemnly swear that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; and that I will obey the orders of the President of the United States and the orders of the officers appointed over me, according to regulations and the Uniform Code of Military Justice. So help me God.

On November 12, 2026, 64 men and women ventured to the Rayburn Office Building of the U.S. Capitol to take that oath and enter the Air Force and Space Force Delayed Entry Program. This swearing-in was the climactic moment of the second annual National Signing Day, an event hosted by the Air Force’s 317th Recruiting Squadron.

The concept of this event came from retired Air Force Master Sergeant and M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins, who said the idea was inspired by watching his son’s announcement for where he was going to play college football.

Wilkins explained, “I was watching this take place and thought to myself, ‘We should be doing something like this for the military.’”

Wilkins’ idea became a reality thanks to several people he worked with, including Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska, Air Force Senior Master Sergeant Matt London, and others within the 317th. It made what was already a significant moment in the lives of these future service members even more memorable for them and their families who accompanied them.

Staff Sergeant Maddalyn Secrist was one of the recruiters on-hand for the event and was very involved with making the 2026 event a success. Secrist shared that having this on Capitol Hill took something local to the DMV area and gave it a sense of national awareness.

“It gives it more of a public view and gives these Airmen and Guardians the recognition that they need.”

Prior to their swearing-in, each person’s name was announced as they went to the table to sign on the dotted line and have their photo taken, reminiscent of the high school athletes who announce where they will play in college. Each new recruit was cheered by family, friends, and fellow American citizens as well as members of the Trump Administration like Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Military Community and Family Policy Stephen B. Simmons and recently appointed Executive Director of the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition, Jacob Phillips.

Among those new recruits was Kevin McAllister, who was one of the older members of the group. At 35 years old and with a family tradition of service, McAllister knew that being physically prepared was a must, which is why he committed to longer runs and more intense training in preparation for the day. He also had to mentally dedicate himself to the process and suggests others who may be considering service do the same.

“I had to find the right mindset. There was a lot of running and calisthenics, but it taught me how to use different muscles,” he said. Even though he was fully prepared to take the oath, being in the Capitol definitely added a level of gravitas to the day.

“We are surrounded by the place where laws are made. The history of the United States is here. Just getting to add this to my family legacy makes me look at the flag differently.”

Bacon addressed the group and offered words of gratitude and encouragement that could be traced back to his own 30-year military career before entering the House of Representatives. He also shared wisdom that could be beneficial to people from all walks of life, whether they are in the military or not.

“Be the best at the job you’re going to get,” Bacon advised. “Learn that job inside and out so your boss can go, ‘I can trust that person.’”

There is no official word on future Signing Day events, but Secrist hopes that recruiters can use highlights or social media posts from this day to inspire their own applicants and create a similar experience to showcase why being a part of the Joint Force is so special.

Secrist said, “We think other recruiters can see this event and get inspired to do something like this in their own squadrons.”

To learn more about the Air Force or Space Force, go to airforce.com or spaceforce.mil.

#8757. Tonal Review (2025): Our Experts Put the Smart Home Gym to the Test

The high-tech home workout system provides a whole-body exercise program.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Jan 29, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Tonal is a high-tech smart gym that makes starting an effective strength workout as easy as stepping into the next room. It has a cable resistance system with multiple attachments, so there is no need for additional equipment. You can choose between instructor-led sessions or work out independently using the demonstrations on the large touchscreen. There are a variety of workouts outside of strength training, including high-intensity interval training (HIIT), cardio, dance, yoga, Pilates, and more.

As a certified personal trainer and wellness product reviewer, I’ve tried (and stopped using) several pieces of home gym equipment. I also work with a team of other expert product reviewers, some of whom have had Tonal for several years and still use it consistently.

This Tonal review describes our experience using it, including details about the equipment, workouts, accessories, and other features. We also spoke to fitness expert Rachael Gonzalez, C.P.T., C.S.C.S., about Tonal’s workout modes and how they can benefit exercisers.

Based on our experience, we give Tonal an overall 5/5 rating. The only category where it didn’t receive a score is assembly, which doesn’t apply since professional installation is required.

Here’s a look at the scoring breakdown on a scale of 1–5:

We’re extremely satisfied with the Tonal equipment and programming. We can get a full workout without taking up a lot of space with free weights or having to pay to go to a gym and leave the house.

The equipment is durable, and we haven’t had any issues. However, moving the arms can be noisy, which may concern people installing it on a shared wall. We had one arm that clicked slightly for a while, but following the troubleshooting instructions on the Tonal website helped fix it.

Some weightlifting moves don’t feel entirely safe or stable, so we usually replace them with ones we’re more comfortable with. The handles, bar, and rope accessories are comfortable to hold and easy to use.

Tonal automatically adjusts weight as you progress, which is really nice. Some workouts have a movement replacement option where you select a modification for the recommended exercise, which has been helpful in certain instances. For example, during pregnancy, you’re supposed to avoid twisting moves, so when one of our testers started lifting after her first trimester, she could easily substitute these moves.

Tonal has worked very well, and one of our testers says it has drastically improved her strength. When she started using Tonal in 2021, she was in the bottom 25 percent of all women. Now, she’s in the top 28 percent, and watching her score increase has motivated her to keep improving.

The Tonal machine is a wall-mounted smart mirror with a built-in touchscreen and two adjustable arms that extend from the sides of the machine and can be moved up and down depending on what exercises you’re doing. You can choose between an on-demand or live instructor-led class or do your own exercises using the Free Lift option. Throughout each class and in Free Lift mode, a trainer explains how to adjust the arms and attach accessories and demonstrates proper form.

Workouts on the built-in workout app include weightlifting exercises such as squats, deadlifts, shoulder presses, lat pulldowns, tricep extensions, curls, and bench presses. The movement library has over 170 exercises to choose from. Each exercise is performed under the resistance of a cable pulley system using a bar, rope, or handle attachment, with up to 100 pounds of resistance per side for a combined 200 pounds.

Tonal recommends weights for each session based on an initial assessment, and your progress and performance determine adjustments. It offers unique weight modes, video form feedback, and floor workouts such as yoga and Pilates. The Tonal app also gives you access to workouts that don’t require the machine arms, so you can work out on the go.

Tonal uses artificial intelligence—Coach AI—to track progress, movement, and data from your workouts to make adjustments, weight recommendations, program suggestions, and more. You don’t have to worry about answering questions like: What do I need to work on today? What weights should I use? Should I focus on my lower body or do a full-body workout? Instead, one tap of the 24-inch touchscreen reveals an interactive library of on-demand and live classes or workout programs. Even in Free Lift mode, an option often used by experienced lifters, Coach AI tracks your data and makes adjustments and weight recommendations.

The first time you use Tonal, you’ll complete the Strength Assessment, which starts by choosing from the following goals:

After selecting your goal, you’ll indicate whether you are a beginner, intermediate, or advanced exerciser and perform several movements—including a seated lat pulldown, seated overhead press, bench press, and neutral grip deadlifts—to help Coach AI get to know you and adapt to your needs, much like an online personal trainer. Your strength assessment results are used by Coach AI as a baseline when selecting the weight for each movement and to recommend workouts and programs.

While this is a good starting point, it could be better. It’s hard to assess your overall fitness based on a single workout—what if you had an off day? Tonal addresses this by learning more about your strength level based on your performance in subsequent workouts and adjusting the weight settings to reflect your strength better.

During daily training sessions, it uses metrics such as time under tension, power output, range of motion, weight, and time to make weight adjustments and measure progress. Coach AI can detect when your form isn’t correct using your positioning, range of motion, and pacing. If it senses uncertain quality, it provides audible and on-screen reminders and feedback or turns off the weight. For example, the resistance shuts off if the bar tilts during a bench press because it suggests the movement is incorrect or unstable. If it senses you are moving the weight too easily, it increases the load each rep so you get the intended stimulus of the workout.

Another impressive feature is the four weight modes: Spotter, Burnout, Chains, and Eccentric. In Spotter mode, Tonal senses when you are struggling with a rep, lowers the weight so you can complete it, and returns the weight for the next rep to re-challenge your strength. Burnout senses fatigue and reduces weight until you finish the set. The Chains mode replicates the feeling of putting chains on the barbell by increasing the resistance during a lift’s concentric or shortening phase. Eccentric increases the resistance as you release the weight for more time under tension, which may help muscle growth.

Tonal enables each mode automatically during live and on-demand workouts. This automation creates a seamless transition between segments like supersets, where you concentrate on opposing muscle groups with little rest in between. If you want to work out with a partner, weight adjustments for both parties are automated.

Experienced experts lead each workout by demonstrating and talking you through set up and proper form. Even if you choose to follow the Free Lift setting or build a custom workout using the extensive movement library, there are video explanations of how to perform each movement. When you enable a specific weight mode, the weight is adjusted automatically, or you can adjust it manually on the screen using the dial. Interestingly, you can adjust the weight in one-pound increments, an uncommon feature in most cable machines and free weights, which typically adjust in 2.5 or five-pound increments.

To access these features, you’ll need a paid membership for $60 monthly, and Tonal requires a subscription for the first year. The only way to use Tonal without the membership is to manually set the weights to perform unguided exercises like a cable machine.

The purchase price of $3,995 includes the machine (which includes the touchscreen and arms) and no accessories. Aside from the floor workouts, most workouts use the arms and attachments, so Tonal isn’t usable without them. While you can use attachments from other brands, you’ll need to purchase T-lock adapters from Tonal for $43.

The smart accessories bundle from Tonal costs $495. If your budget allows, I recommend buying it because it includes everything you need to start using your Tonal immediately. Each accessory is available separately, so you can also choose what works best for you. Here’s a breakdown of what the bundle includes and pricing for each item individually:

The smart accessories have a safety feature to turn the weight on and off with a button rather than by touching the screen, so you can position yourself before loading. The handles have a button on the side that’s easy to reach while gripping, and the rope and bar come with an attachable clip.

As a beginner, our tester initially thought working out with Tonal was intimidating, but it’s a simple process once you learn how the smart home gym works. With a membership, you can choose between live and on-demand classes or a progressive program. Based on your Strength Score established in the initial assessment, the recommended weights are set automatically for you.

From there, you follow the trainer’s instructions and on-screen prompts to set the arms and choose the right accessories for each move. Tonal automatically adjusts the weight, counts reps, and provides form feedback as you progress through the workout. There’s even an audible cue when you have two reps left, so you know what to expect if you’re facing away from the machine.

Free Lift allows you to choose from the library of movements and do as many sets and reps as you’d like. Much like the classes, the screen displays your live stats, and you receive a workout summary with your time under tension, range of motion, power output, and total volume lifted.

You can do floor workouts such as cardio, yoga, and barre directly on Tonal or by using the Tonal app on another device.

Strength training is the main draw of Tonal, so most of Tonal’s content focuses on weightlifting and HIIT training with weights. In addition to the four weight modes mentioned earlier, there are two custom modes:

Gonzalez says these options add variety and challenge, enhancing strength gains and training overall. “Diversification in your routine keeps you engaged and introduces new challenges,” she says. “Plus, variation can help you push past a training plateau.”

Trainer-led workouts on Tonal automatically implement these modes depending on the intended stimuli, but you can activate them manually in the settings for any workout. You can adjust the weight at any point during your workout using the dial on the screen.

“When training, I’m always super mindful of how my body feels and take it easy when I need to, so the Recovery Mode option would work well for when you’re sore or just want to move,” Gonzalez says. “I really like the eccentric-focused mode. During the eccentric portion of a rep, the muscle lengthens while under tension,” she says. “The eccentric portion of a lift occurs when you are lowering the weight, moving against the opposing force of gravity, and research shows controlled lengthening of the muscle fibers contributes to overall strength and muscle development.”

In addition, there are several other types of workouts available on Tonal, including:

Tonal has a massive catalog of guided workouts and workout programs and a library of over 200 bodyweight moves to allow you to build custom workouts.

The guided programs range from three to five weeks and focus on goals like improving overall fitness, gaining lean muscle mass, and burning fat. For example, Fundamentally Fit guides you through basic movement patterns, and House of Volume uses progressive overload to build strength. Many users on Reddit recommend Four Weeks to Fat Loss, a combination of resistance training and HIIT to maximize energy output. One says, “Four Weeks to Fat Loss did amazing things to my body composition! Doing that program was when I really started to see a difference in how my clothes fit.”

The smart handles help replicate moves performed with dumbbells and kettlebells, like hammer curls, bicep curls, or goblet squats. The smart rope can copy moves with a rope or chains, like pull-throughs or tricep extensions. Finally, the bar can replicate barbell moves such as deadlifts and bench presses. You can purchase accessories from another brand, but the smart accessories bundle from Tonal has Bluetooth connectivity, so you can press a single button on the accessory to turn the weight on or off.

If you buy third-party accessories, you must purchase T-locks from Tonal to attach them securely. Additionally, you’ll need to turn the weight on and off directly on the touchscreen.

Tonal has a roster of expert instructors based in its New York studio and guest coaches who occasionally provide unique content. These fitness experts have diverse backgrounds, from competitive athletes to sports medicine.

All Tonal-created workouts are instructor-led, so you’ll hear tips about form and safety throughout. Each instructor brings a unique style, personality, and expertise to the table, and Tonal users generally find instructors they prefer. For many, this provides the experience of working with a personal trainer, and several of Tonal’s past and current coaches offer personal training services outside of Tonal. For these reasons, Tonal allows you to filter workouts by instructor.

The Tonal app allows you to access your workout history, create workouts, and do floor workouts directly from your phone. The only thing you can’t do on the Tonal app is weightlifting workouts that require using the resistance cables.

In addition, Tonal connects to several fitness apps, including Apple Health, Google Fit, and Strava. It also syncs with several heart rate monitors using Bluetooth, and you can connect to your Amazon Music or Apple Music account to stream or choose from the 14 stations on Tonal Radio.

Tonal has several features to help keep members engaged with the community and the equipment.

First, there are several achievements you can earn for performing certain types of workouts, working out on holidays or birthdays, or reaching milestones like weekly streaks or 1,000,000 pounds lifted. Your workout summary lists the badges and milestones reached and your progress toward the following milestones. The Total Achievements Card shows how many workouts you’ve finished, the pounds you’ve lifted, and the longest weekly streak you’ve completed. You earn badges by trying a new workout type, training consistently, and working out at a different time of day. These achievements can be shared with friends and family using the mobile app.

The Tonal Leaderboard ranks all active exercisers based on how many days or hours they’ve used Tonal in the last 30 days, so the more you train, the higher you’ll rank.

Your Strength Score increases from the baseline as you get stronger and demonstrate progress during workouts. These improvements are calculated based on your historical workout data and are a huge source of motivation for many Tonal users. Using a percentage-based comparison, you can see how your Strength Score ranks against others, so some friendly competition is involved.

Tonal has a very active social media community if you prefer direct interaction with other members. The brand’s private Facebook community, The Official Tonal Community (OTC), has over 53,000 members and regularly hosts workout challenges and live discussions with Tonal trainers.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years, and she’s used it consistently the entire time, only stepping away briefly for injury recovery and pregnancy.

Before Tonal, despite being fully aware of the benefits of resistance training, she had no weightlifting experience beyond the occasional half-hearted kettlebell or dumbbell workout.

Tonal takes all the guesswork out of resistance training so you can lift the weights and reap the benefits, which is our favorite thing about it. You don’t have to worry about setting weights, planning workouts, increasing weights or reps, or tracking your progress.

At first, our tester didn’t understand Tonal’s difficulty levels. She thought the Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced class levels aligned with strength and fitness experience, but they correlate with the technicality of the moves involved. Beginner classes may include heavy weights if recommended by your Strength Score and the algorithm. The “beginner” aspect is that the workout moves are less technical, making effective strength training accessible to those who might typically be considered “casual” fitness enthusiasts.

Our tester says Tonal is a lot of fun. She’s discovered she loves lifting weights, and when she misses a few workouts, she gets antsy about getting started again. Tonal introduced her to barre, a ballet-inspired floor workout she’s grown to adore. There aren’t many new floor workouts, which is sad because she loves the barre and pre/postnatal classes.

Our tester has attended live classes, but she doesn’t very often. Sometimes, she struggles with the pacing for floor/cardio workouts but finds the weightlifting workouts easy to follow. Mostly, she sticks to on-demand workouts because she appreciates the guided warm-up, exercise, and cool-down.

One concern users in the Tonal Facebook community raise is the lead trainer demonstrates the moves during a live workout, which is not true for on-demand classes. These workouts use the lead trainer’s voiceover and cut to another trainer demonstrating the exercises. This inconsistency doesn’t bother us, but some say it disrupts their flow or makes it harder to follow.

The instructors showcase their personalities, and none of the workouts our tester watched seem overly scripted or cheesy. Tonal recently moved their studio from California to New York and replaced the coaching staff. Our reviewer had grown accustomed to the “old” coaches and still gravitates toward their workouts because she likes their calm demeanor. Some coaches have a bubbly, energetic coaching style, and others take a tough-love approach.

These trainers have diverse professional backgrounds to support the workouts they design. For example, when our tester’s doctor cleared her to work out after a knee injury, she found Coach Liz’s workouts helpful because the coach is also a physical therapist.

Our tester completed several of the guided programs and saw consistent strength gains from each program. The programs can get repetitive, though, since many of them repeat the same two or three workouts for the duration of the program.

When our tester started using Tonal, her Strength Score was 133, and she was in one of the lowest percentiles of all female Tonal members. Although her progress has been slow, her Strength Score is now 354, and according to Tonal, she’s stronger than 82 percent of all female users. Something about getting higher and higher in those percentiles is supremely motivating for her. In addition to her soaring strength, she’s experienced improvements in her mobility and range of motion.

The base price of Tonal is $3,995, and the optional smart accessories bundle (which we highly recommend purchasing) is an additional $495. Professional installation, which is required, costs $295. Several users on Reddit report signing a Release of Liability waiver and installing it themselves, but there is no option to remove the installation charge at checkout. Tonal often runs promotions and offers free shipping and installation.

A subscription is required for the first year and costs $60 per month. You can discontinue the membership after one year, but you’ll lose access to many features.

If you purchase Tonal, the optional smart accessories bundle, and the required one-year subscription, the total cost of Tonal within the first year is roughly $5,500 before taxes, not including delivery and installation.

A monthly subscription costs $60 per month and isn’t technically required after you’ve completed your first year of membership.

You can only use Tonal as a cable machine for free lift workouts, and without a membership, you won’t have access to any Tonal content, weight modes, workout or strength data, history, or custom workouts.

The Tonal website says professional installation is required. Before purchasing, you’ll need to complete a survey providing additional information for the installers, such as where to set up Tonal and the stud spacing in your walls.

If they determine you don’t have an appropriate place to install it, there are solutions. The brand offers wide-mount adapter bars and installation kits for metal studs. If you have concerns about where you can have Tonal installed, contact the brand’s customer service team for help. Typically, installation fees are $295, but Tonal occasionally offers free delivery and installation.

If you move, you’ll need to schedule a professional reinstallation. Tonal offers relocation packages for moving homes or simply relocating furniture to another room. Relocation fees range from $300 to $500 plus taxes, depending on your chosen service.

Tonal does not cover damage caused by attempting to install or reinstall the home gym, and if you choose this option, Tonal requests you sign a Release of Liability waiver.

Tonal offers a two-year limited warranty on the trainer and touchscreen, which covers parts, shipping, and labor. The smart accessories have a one-year warranty for parts plus shipping and labor. For such a premium (and expensive) piece of equipment, a five-year warranty on the device would be nice—and more comparable to warranties offered by other premium fitness equipment brands.

Tonal customers have had mixed experiences with customer service. Some say customer service quickly and competently addressed their concerns, while others say they needed more urgency from the customer service team.

The Tonal website has several glowing reviews from its users, many of whom say they have canceled their gym memberships while drastically improving their strength and fitness levels. Several reviewers are excited about their progress and enjoy the objective tracking data from workouts.

Tonal has a 2.⅖ on Trustpilot. Several critical reviews mention installation, maintenance, and customer service issues. Tonal partners with a third-party company for delivery, installation, and repairs, and many concerns center around problems with this specific company rather than Tonal itself. Positive reviews mention the variety of workouts, convenience, and ease of use.

People on Reddit say they work out more frequently with Tonal and enjoy the extra time saved from skipping gym commutes. Several mention the cable resistance feels heavier than free weights, so the maximum poundage is not a limiting factor. One user says they wish to see a floor-based alternative in the future for those who rent or need to move.

Tonal is ideal for people who are interested in weightlifting but need guidance and support to get started and see results. It’s a great fit for athletes and highly active people who want to advance in strength training to support their athletic endeavors and fitness goals.

Likewise, many dedicated weightlifters have switched from using free weights to this comprehensive, versatile system. Tonal is an excellent option if you dislike going to the gym and prefer an all-in-one home gym solution.

Tonal isn’t ideal for people outfitting their home gym on a limited budget. For Tonal’s high price tag, you could buy a complete set of dumbbells or other free weights and other equipment or pay for several years of a gym membership.

Additionally, Tonal likely won’t be a good fit for advanced weight lifters already at or near the maximum of 100 pounds per arm offered for many lifts.

This machine requires adequate space to extend the arms to fully perform all necessary movements. If you live in a small or cramped space, it may not work for you.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years. Here are some of the criteria she used to evaluate Tonal when she first received it, and which are still very important to her two years later:

Tonal and Peloton are very different but complement one another in several ways. Many Tonal users are also Peloton users since Tonal covers the strength training aspect, while the Peloton bike, treadmill, and rower provide heart-pumping cardio workouts. Each app offers live classes, and the monthly subscription to the Peloton App+ is $24, and Tonal costs $60.

The Peloton App One—$12.99 monthly—houses the brand’s floor workouts and has a much larger and more frequently updated library than the Tonal app. Peloton may work better if you enjoy these classes more than weightlifting. It’s more budget-friendly than Tonal, but Tonal offers a more comprehensive strength training system and programming.

Tempo is a smart strength training system and one of Tonal’s major competitors. It utilizes free weights outfitted with sensors rather than Tonal’s electromagnetic cable system.

The Tempo Move—an equipment package with 16 weight plates ideal for beginner and intermediate use and a 12-month Tempo membership—starts at $963. It’s a more accessible system for people with limited budgets and has advanced features such as rep counting and monitoring form. Tester Jordan Smith, C.P.T., says, “It did a great job counting my reps, but it didn’t always pick up on my form.”

The Tempo Move does not come with a screen, so you have to use your phone or other device, whereas Tonal has a dedicated workout space to stream workouts from an app. The Tempo Studio has a 42-inch display and ranges from $2,963–$4,463, depending on your accessory package.

Tonal can be incredible for your health, providing the structure and convenience needed to start and stick to a strength training routine. The fun programming, smart weight recommendations, and space-saving home gym setup make it a worthwhile investment for anyone interested in increasing their strength and who can fit it wisely into their budget.

Yes, after the first year. The $60/month subscription begins at installation and is mandatory for the first 12 months you own the machine. After one year, you can pause or cancel your subscription, and Tonal functions in “Basic Free Lift” mode, where you guide your own workouts. You can’t access your data analytics, workout content, or dynamic weight modes that provide personal training features.

Choosing between Tonal or free weights is a personal choice. Tonal has some pros: It’s space-saving and sets your weight based on your current strength level. Free weights are less expensive and don’t require an internet connection.

Currently, a Tonal membership costs $60 per month. Without the membership fee, Tonal works similarly to a manual cable machine.

Tonal weight feels up to 26 percent heavier than standard weights, according to one Tonal-affiliated study. The weight generated on Tonal maintains resistance throughout the entire rep, unlike free weights, which can feel lighter due to momentum and working with gravity at specific parts of the rep rather than against it.

No, Tonal is an independent company and is not affiliated with Peloton.

No, Tonal requires a WiFi connection, even if you don’t have a paid Tonal membership.

Tonal smart equipment seamlessly integrates with the base Tonal model. If you wish to use your own exercise equipment, you can purchase special adapters from Tonal.

#8756. JJ Spaun Got His Swing Back After a Misdiagnosis Nearly Wrecked His PGA Career

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

PGA star John Michael “JJ” Spaun has been at home with the golf clubs since he was gifted that first plastic toy set at age 3. But while the young protégé followed in his mother’s golf-playing footsteps, and furthered them by making progress in the PGA, a mysterious health issue would begin to derail his game.

Spaun sat down with M&F to discuss his initial Type 2 diabetes diagnosis, and how finally being discovered as Type 1 brought him back to greener pastures.

“I would say, in the majority, golf was a pretty easy sport for me to pick up,” says Spaun. “But I think I battled with what time and effort I wanted to put into it as a kid. Growing up in Southern California, other sports were pulling me in. Skateboarding was a huge presence at the time. I wanted to do what the other kids were doing culturally, which was skateboarding and extreme sports.”

In his youth, Spaun played a variety of sports aside from golf, including skateboarding, bicycling, baseball, basketball, and hockey. But while he did eventually fully embrace golf, his other experiences began to pay off. “I think those sports all played a role in my development, in my mechanics,” says Spaun. “Like hand-eye coordination, footwork. My swing coach, who I have been with for around six years, is a firm believer that skateboarding really developed my footwork for my golf swing even as a child. He considers my feet to be my superpower.”

JJ Spaun has just completed his 10th season with the PGA. He turned professional in 2012 and earned his first PGA Tour Card in 2016, but the players’ game began to take a downturn in 2018. He struggled with consistency and even lost his tour card during the 2020-21 season, where he placed 174th in the FedEx Cup rankings. Since the summer of 2018, Spaun found himself almost unable to complete a round of golf.

“I was 28 at the time,” he recalls. “I remember putting on my belt and running out of holes to put the notch in, so my belt was now too big for me. I suffered with severe thirst at night, and then frequently urinating, like, three or four times every night. I started losing weight very rapidly.”

Initially chalking all this up to a demanding golf season, Spaun decided to see a doctor after weighing himself and realizing that he’d inexplicably lost another 20 pounds in just a couple of months. The athlete was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes and hoped that the treatment would help him return to his prior form on the golf course. But that wasn’t to be.

“After three years, losing 50 pounds, going down to 155 pounds, I hadn’t weighed that since high school, so I finally got advice from an endocrinologist,” shares Spaun, who was then diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes, rather than Type 2.

Sadly, with 90% of diabetes sufferers having Type 2, medical advances for detecting Type 1 have been slower to emerge. Type 2 is often triggered by obesity, whereas Type 1 is thought to be more of a genetic issue causing the immune system to attack insulin producing cells in the pancreas. “They felt sorry for me, telling me that I was Type 1, but I said this is great, because I’ve been living miserably,” says Spaun. “My energy was at an all-time low. My golf was going down the drain. And now I had a real solution.”

Finally gaining the correct diagnosis in 2021, Spaun started insulin therapy. “In a matter of weeks, I could feel the strength coming back,” says the top golfer. “I was able to eat things without restricting my glucose range, as you do with Type 2. I started to feel better and things started coming together.”

Losing so much weight took time to overcome, however. “Your mechanics and your movements are off,” explains Spaun. “I’m glad to be handling things well. It’s definitely a challenge, but I’ve got all the support in the world to really make it as easy for me as possible.”

Incredibly, with the weight coming back and his treatment working well, Spaun had his breakthrough season in 2025, including a major victory at the 125th US Open. Spaun tells M&F that he uses a Dexcom G7 continuous glucose monitor to keep his levels in check and has recently switched from insulin injections to a pump system known as the Omnipod 5. “It’s been a game changer for me,” he shares.

In September 2026, Spaun was also able combine his love of traveling to England with his passion for golf, winning the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, and even donating a portion of his winnings to the Addington Fund, a British Charity that supports farming families. The golfer tells M&F that he discovered the financial hardships that many UK farms face during his holidays in the Cotswolds, where discovered the popular Prime series, Clarkson’s Farm.

“I’m the type of guy that likes to put in the work, because I’m a strong believer that you get out of this game what you put in,” says Spaun. But with the official season now over, the able athlete can look ahead to more family time, and another trip back to England.

No doubt, JJ Spaun is a highly decorated athlete with an even promising future, but living with diabetes has taught him that being present in the moment is more important than any trophy, so we conclude our interview and Spaun heads out on the school run.

#8755. Hyatt Category 4 Free Night Certificate — Card Perk Sweet Spot

The simplest high-value card perk in travel rewards — no points math required

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

The core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

Hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or New Year's Eve.

Your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

The pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

This matters for your broader strategy. Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

Log in to your World of Hyatt account at hyatt.com and navigate to your account dashboard. Under the "My Certificates & Awards" section, confirm your Category 1–4 free night certificate is present and note its expiration date. Certificates are typically valid for 12 months from issuance, so don't let it sit unused. If you don't see it and you've crossed the $15,000 annual spend threshold on your World of Hyatt Credit Card, allow a few days for it to post after your statement closes, or call Chase to confirm.

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability shows for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

Hyatt award availability at popular properties can be limited during peak periods. Your tactical options:

Your free night certificate works at all of them equally. Unlike hotel programs with dynamic pricing where the cost of a free night fluctuates with demand, Hyatt's fixed chart means you can target the highest-value Category 4 properties without paying more. Your certificate covers one night. If you're staying multiple nights, stack it strategically: apply the certificate to the highest-cost night (often a Saturday) and book the remaining nights with World of Hyatt points transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This hybrid approach maximizes the value of every currency you're using.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. As a cardholder, your spending activity resets this clock automatically. But if you ever pause card use, make a small Hyatt purchase — even a $1 on-property charge — to reset the timer and protect your balance.

This sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. If your annual spending is significantly below $15,000 on a single card, this particular mechanism won't trigger. In that case, the World of Hyatt Credit Card still earns Hyatt points on spending and delivers a Category 1–4 certificate on each card anniversary — so it retains value, just through a different path. Also, if you're deeply committed to a non-Hyatt hotel program, the benefit is obviously less useful without a library of Hyatt properties in your regular rotation.

## Rated: Easy (4/5 Beginner Friendly) This is one of the most accessible sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem, and that's by design. The certificate mechanism removes the two biggest friction points in traditional points redemptions: **finding the right number of points** and **navigating complex transfer timing**. #8753. How Reverse-Grip Lat Pulldowns Helped Jay Cutler Build an Even Wider Back

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Mass monster Jay Cutler, who claimed the title of Mr. Olympia on four occasions between 2006 and 2010, was never afraid to step away from the barbell if there was an efficient way to sculpt his back. Recently, the bodybuilder revealed that he liked to begin each back session with cable reverse-grip pulldowns. Here’s why.

“This was always the first exercise I started my back routine with,” confirmed Cutler in a recent video for his 5.7 million IG followers.

Techniques used by Jay Cutler to string together 25 consecutive top 2 finishes.

Utilizing a supinated (underhand) grip, you’ll primarily tax the lats while also recruiting the biceps and mid back. For many, the supinated grip is more comfortable on the shoulders than the pronated (overhand) grip. So, seated at the cable station, you’ll replicate a similar movement with the upper body to a chin up as you lower the bar. This grip also allows for heavier loads, making it perfect for adding upper body mass.

Tip: Keep your torso still and pull with the elbows until the bar is lowered just under your chin. Don’t pull any further down, or the load will shift to your forearms and shoulders.

“When you do something, reverse grip, it’s going to give you more flexion in those lats. It’s going to allow you to pull a little deeper and engage certain fibers,” explained Cutler who, as a competitive bodybuilder, was all about lifting heavy weights to create a winning physique.

In his video, Cutler kept the distance between his hands a little over shoulder width. “Pull down, focus on 12 repetitions,” he added. The Olympia icon also explained that the reverse grip lat pulldown was essential to building the winged appearance of his lats. “So, when I was doing that front double bicep (pose), it really yanked those lats out,” shared the legend. “And created that great V-taper.”

For Jay Cutler, the reverse grip lat pulldown was key to building muscle thickness. To try it for yourself, avoid using momentum and concentrate on the muscle contraction instead, as you lower the bar. Then slowly allow the bar to return skywards for additional time under tension.

#8752. ‘Just a Guy With a Boat on His Head’: He’s Running 52 Marathons in 52 Weeks—While Carrying a Canoe Every Step

Travis Meier wants people talking about protecting public lands. His approach is making waves.

Getting to the Philadelphia Marathon on November 22 proved an endurance event of its own for Travis Meier. The 38-year-old Minneapolis resident flew into Hartford, Connecticut, drove three hours into the Adirondack Mountains to pick up a canoe, then spent another five hours behind the wheel getting to Philadelphia. This was all before tackling Sunday’s 26.2 miles with the boat balanced over his head.

And yes, the canoe made it through the entire race without ever touching water.

“Coming from Minnesota, I can't just throw a boat in an overhead compartment," Meier told Runner's World. "It was a logistical nightmare: where to keep it, where to sneak it into the race, and how people would react to it."

Despite the travel headaches, Meier came away from Philadelphia with his second personal record in as many weeks. It was another step in his latest undertaking: 52 marathons in 52 weeks, each while carrying a canoe, to raise awareness about protecting the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in northern Minnesota.

Meier, who manages a distillery when he isn't hauling boats around, wasn't exactly a seasoned runner when all this started. His introduction to the sport came through the Red Bull Urban Portage, an event that involved carrying a boat through downtown Minneapolis before paddling along the Mississippi River.

“I was really bad at paddling, but I could outrun people,” he recalled. Before the event, he bought a Northstar ADK canoe off Craigslist with every intention of selling it once the race was over. Instead, it found a home on his garage wall and managed to stick around for another year. Eventually, he started entering more races with it.

That eventually brought him to Minnesota's Ely Marathon in 2023, where he completed his first-ever 26.2-mile race while carrying a canoe. Since then, he's run only one conventional marathon without a boat, and what started solely as a personal experiment gradually became an opportunity to draw attention to a place he'd loved for years.

The Boundary Waters, a wilderness area known for its lakes, forests, and extensive canoe routes, has been at the center of a contentious debate over proposed mining operations. Federal protections restricting mining in the surrounding watershed were rolled back earlier this year, a development that particularly frustrated Meier.

"I've been to many remote places on this earth, and very few have its caliber of perfect,” he said. “So why would someone want to mess it up?"

Meier had been toying with the idea of running 52 marathons in 52 weeks ever since reading about Dane Rauschenberg, who accomplished the feat in 2006. With the ongoing fight over protections for the Boundary Waters, he had his reason to give it a shot, bringing his canoe as a form of protest to May’s Taco Bell 50K. It got people asking questions, which was exactly what he wanted, and gave him encouragement to keep showing up at races with a boat on his head.

Of course, carrying a canoe for more than four hours at a time comes with some challenges, particularly when Mother Nature gets involved.

During the Mankato Marathon in Minnesota, Meier battled 30mph winds along a ridge beside a cornfield. Mile 14 alone took him nearly 22 minutes, as his canoe repeatedly caught the wind and spun him around like a kite.

At one point, Meier turned to a few supporters witnessing him get thrown around and asked, “When's the point of insanity?” He sent them ahead to see if the wind conditions were better ahead in the valley. Luckily, the gusts let up enough, sparing him a repeat trip through that nightmare.

The spectators in Philadelphia offered a different kind of entertainment, with plenty to say about the guy running a marathon with a canoe on his head.

Around mile three, Meier encountered a young girl who appeared scared by the enormous object approaching her. He knelt down, giving her enough confidence to return his high-five.

"Grandmas confess their love to me, and I don't know why," he said of his interactions with spectators, adding that Philadelphia set a record for the number of phallic jokes he heard along the course.

The jokes are part of the experience, and the attention is ultimately what he's hoping for. Meier said fellow runners often approach him after a race to discuss the Boundary Waters and the larger issue of protecting public lands. He's also seen Instagram comments from people who knew little about the area before coming across his videos.

"They may not know anything, but they've at least gotten a 10,000-foot view of the BWCA," he said.

The running community has helped make the challenge possible, with sponsors pitching in for race entries and shoes while Meier covers the remaining expenses. He's even promised to refund their donations if he doesn't complete the challenge.

"My integrity is everything,” he said, “even though I'm not a company, just a guy with a boat on his head.”

His biggest sacrifice so far has been giving up so much of his free time. Between a full-time job, travel, recovery, and the weekly races, there’s no room for a vacation abroad. He has considered tackling back-to-back marathons to create some breathing room. His body hasn't agreed to the arrangement.

As for what would make all 52 races worthwhile, Meier has a specific outcome in mind: permanent legislation protecting the Boundary Waters. Here’s the good news: proposals exist in both the House of Representatives and Senate. Even so, he knows that may be a tall order. But his presence—and effort—are creating awareness.

"If it doesn't happen, which it likely won't, at least the effort started conversations about our public lands," he said.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.
