#8724. Andrew Jacked Shares His Back-Building Training Ahead of the Arnold Classic

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

With fans and competitors now looking to the 2027 Arnold Classic for the next big battle of the bodybuilding titans, last year’s winner could take to the stage with an even more impressive back. Recently, Chinedu Andrew Obiekea, who is better known to flex fans as “Andrew Jacked,” shared his training process—and it was boss level.

Undoubtedly, 2026 was a breakout year for the Nigerian French competitor. First, Jacked won the biggest prize in bodybuilding history, picking up a check for $750,000 for winning the Arnold Classic in Columbus, Ohio. Then days later, the big man won the Arnold UK, and picked up another $250,000 for his efforts. But with current and former Mr. Olympia’s like Nick Walker, Hadi Choopan, and potentially Samson Dauda hot on his heels, AJ is now in the process of jacking up his back to maintain his top position with the judges.

AJ jolts his back to adapt with this simple but seriously heavy workout.

“Yesszziirrr!!!,” came the trademark quote from AJ, as he shared his herculean efforts for more than a million followers on Instagram. Here’s how to try it for yourself:

AJ began with an unorthodox but rewarding version of the bent over row. Rather than use a dumbbell or barbell, the “Mona Lisa of bodybuilding,” stood behind the chest support on a T-bar row machine, gripping the frame for support, while taxing his working arm independently. By following the strict path of the machine, AJ maximized the load and strengthened his middle and lower trapezius (below his neck), while also building thickness in the side of his back working the lats and teres minor and major.

With his back now suitably blasted, Jacked continued the onslaught with the traditional standing barbell bent over row. Using a pronated (overhand) grip, AJ once again targeted the lats while also building his mid and upper back. Next up was the chest supported mid row, zeroing in on the upper back, including the traps and rhomboids (located between the shoulder blades and spine) Notice, in all of Andrew Jacked’s movements, how he likes to extend his arms to the very bottom of each lift, in order to find a maximum stretch before contracting his gigantic muscles. The lats then took another licking with cable lat pulldowns, while seated cable rows hit all the major muscle groups in the back.

To strengthen his posterior chain, Jacked performs back extensions at a 45-degree angle, building the entire back, glutes, and even his hamstrings. This exercise is particularly savvy, because it supports lumbar stability, improves hip mobility, and means that his other lifts may benefit while maintaining longevity to boot. To work his back even harder, the 2026 Arnold Classic champ pics up some weight plates to take with him on each extension.

When you attack the back from all angles, you will also recruit additional muscles, so to round out his session, Jacked focuses on his already stimulated biceps, and reps out some preacher curls to isolate his arms into exhaustion.

To try this workout for yourself, aim for 8 to 12 reps and perform 2 to 3 sets of each exercise. For the back extensions, start out without the extra weight, and bring it on when you feel comfortable. Yesszziirrr!

#8723. In Praise of the Charity Ride, One of the Most Underrated Ways to Tackle Your First Century—or Any Big Cycling Goal

They say pride comes before the fall. In cycling, I’ve found pride usually comes before the first true descent.

I relearned this lesson earlier this month, when I found myself at the top of Bear Mountain, the only notable multi-mile climb close enough to bike to from New York City. Its peak was situated about halfway into the 105-mile route of the Best Buddies Challenge New York, an event the organization had brought back for a second year to fund its programming for teenagers and young adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. The riders gawking at the intermittently vermilion canopy who were pedaling alongside me had each raised at least $1,800 to reach this particular vista, plus access to several deliciously well-stocked aid stations, SAG vehicles, and the promise of a raucous finish-line party.

Though I’m relatively new to road cycling, I’ve done some long gravel rides and recently tackled the Maratona dles Dolomites in Italy, where I buried myself to finish a 66-mile route that featured over 10,000 feet of elevation and one 8-mile climb up the Passo Valparolo. By comparison, the Best Buddies Challenge century, with 2,000 fewer feet of climbing stretched over a much longer route, seemed plenty doable when I signed up in September.

The first indication I had erred came before I had pinned my bib number to my jersey. At a pre-ride reception, I sat down with Alberto Contador (yes, that Alberto Contador), who was returning to the event for the second time. He was confident I could handle Bear Mountain, but warned me that the end of the ride reminded him of La Flèche Wallonne, a notoriously difficult Belgian one-day race known for its repeat ascents of the relatively short, brutally steep Mur de Huy. “The last 30 miles is all up and down…save energy,” he said.

By the time I slid into the fourth aid station, which marked the 33-miles-to-go point in my own ride, this advice was well out of my mind. I was supremely confident in my ability to finish strong. Sure, I had gone a bit deeper in the tank to maintain contact with random groups throughout the day in valleys and on shallow sections, but there was so little left to go.

The Best Buddies Challenge is relatively new to New York City, but the concept of the charity ride is not. The Five Boro Bike Tour, which raises money for Bike New York’s free education and mechanics program, has given city cyclists the chance to experience streets without car traffic since 1977. On the West Coast, Washington’s Cascade Bicycle Club’s Seattle to Portland Bicycle Classic now generates about $1 million each year to fund the organization’s community programs, cycling education, and statewide cycling advocacy work. Even the ride I did in the Dolomites this summer offers charity entrants, who have, over the years, raised over $2 million for road safety, food security, disease research, and rural education.

Among non-endurance athletes, these rides often draw comparisons to running events like the New York City Marathon. There are certainly similarities—sanctioned routes, feed stations, distances that sound absurd to normies—but cyclists don’t tend to give even long charity rides anything close to the same level of credence as runners do to marathons.

That kind of resistance perhaps comes from those strains of cycling tradition that prize grit and ardor and self-reliance. Conquering Mur de Huy during a race takes superhuman levels of tenacity and determination—charity rides, by contrast, even those that span 100 miles, are much more comfortable affairs. Do some riders dismiss these events because they’re too soft? It’s possible.

Beginner-friendliness is often baked into the event programming of charity rides. Breakthrough T1D Rides, held to fund research for type 1 diabetes, are actually four-day retreats. Participants spend only one day on the bike. Anthony Geraci, national director of Ride & Endurance Programs, says most of these rides feature “out-and-back” courses. Turn around whenever you feel done with your day! “We always say it’s not about the miles, it’s about the mission.”

Sure, you could cross-stitch that phrase onto a throw pillow. But it’s also the kind of mentality that cyclists might need to achieve some personal goals, whether that’s riding in a new destination or tackling their first century. In this way, charity rides can be catalysts for remarkable personal achievement.

They also create the conditions for extremely impressive fundraising. Best Buddies International CEO Anthony Shriver (yes, that Shriver) told me that its cycling events account for about 10 to 15 percent of the organization’s annual revenue. Similarly, Kris Rauh, vice president, event experience and operations for NMSS, says its 49 Bike MS events generate about $52 million in revenue annually for the organization.

Indeed, she continued, many of the people signing up to do their first Bike MS have no personal connection to the disease in its name. “They come to us mostly because they want a challenge on a bike … they don’t come to us as fundraisers,” she said.

For charity rides like Bike MS and Best Buddies, it’s important to connect participants to their mission and the impact of their work. As I ascended Bear Mountain and pushed myself on the way back, I wasn’t just riding with Contador and Chris Froome (who was also participating this year) but also plenty of folks who volunteer for or participate in Best Buddies programming. In fact, individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities often held key roles during its rides. At the Challenge New York, a “Buddy” gave a speech while we waited in the start pen, a different “Buddy” sang the national anthem, and still others staffed the aid stations. “From the moment you wake up at 4 o’clock in the morning, you should know you’re doing something that’s going to enrich another human being’s life,” Shriver said.

The combination makes these kinds of charity rides feel a lot different than a standard criterium or gravel fondo. And it seems to hold enough appeal to keep the organizations hosting them going. Best Buddies, which has substantial fundraising minimums for riders, gets a 30 to 50 percent return rate, Shriver says. According to Rauh, at Bike MS that number is closer to 60 percent. That’s a lot of people returning to charity rides each year.

About two-thirds of the way into my own New York Challenge, I was actively questioning how this could be possible. Though I had been correct that all the long climbs were behind me, the “rolling” terrain I had imagined was actually a freak show of sharp pitches. I cracked on a climb my Garmin did not categorize, attempting to hold serve over a bump with a gradient of 18 percent.

I unclipped and shuffled my cramping legs up the embarrassingly short walk to the summit. I felt ashamed by the level of hubris I had brought into the event. If it had been just a regular ride, or even a race, this might have been my day. With hours left to a finish that I felt confident most of the participants had already crossed, it would have been totally within my prerogative to pull the quick-release lever off my front wheel and stuff my bike in a Lyft bound back to Brooklyn.

But as I munched on some blissfully salty crackers that quieted my screaming hamstrings, I realized that getting to the end would be an accomplishment for me regardless of how fast I was able to do it. And, importantly, my path to the shuttle bus that would take me back to the city included one final rest stop. Resolved never to underestimate a “ride” again, I got back in the saddle and held the limpest zone 1 pace of my life until I had made it to the aforementioned support tent. With less than 10 miles left, I slumped into a folding chair and sucked down a can of Sprite.

Immediately, I was engaged by Matt, who was participating in the ride as a volunteer. He asked if I was okay, and when it was clear that I was mentally wrecked, but physically fine, gently encouraged me to get moving. With Matt, another volunteer named Ian, and a pair of other riders who had also had similarly tough days, we set off on the last stretch to the end.

Chatting in my bunch, really the only bunch I had been able to hang on to the entire day, made the miles go by faster and the remaining climbs feel shorter. And when the sugar from my soda hit, I realized I was actually less dead than the pair of participants I had just encountered. Ian and I forged ahead, buoyed by the knowledge the end was near. I managed to stay upright enough up the finishing hill to attempt a celebratory pose as I crossed over the finish line: ninth to last. It was the longest ride I’ve ever done and it challenged me to push myself harder than I might otherwise have done. That’s worth something.

Does anyone have a cool $2,000 I could use to try again next year?

#8721. How Kate Mihevc Edwards Built the Running App That Every Injured Runner Needed

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The moment you can’t do the thing you love most is the moment you understand how much it defines you.

Kate Mihevc Edwards, DPT, has spent more than 16 years watching that moment play out in her clinic. Runners walk in after seeing two, three, sometimes five other providers, still without answers, still hurting, still searching. The problem, she says, has almost never been the injury itself.

“Runners kept finding that they weren’t getting the information they needed,” says Edwards. “They searched everywhere, asked so many people, went to so many providers. And the reason was fragmentation. Nobody was talking. Nobody was working together.”

Edwards is the founder of Precision Performance and Physical Therapy in Atlanta, Director of the Medical Team for the Atlanta Track Club Elite and the creator of RunSource, an expert-filtered running health app launched in June 2026. She did not set out to build an app. She set out to solve a problem she had been watching for over a decade, and the app became the only solution that made sense at scale.

The evidence for what she was building came from the Atlanta Track Club. Six years ago, Edwards helped construct a fully integrated medical team for the club’s elite athletes: physical therapists, a sports dietitian, a sports psychologist, a mental performance coach, a chiropractor and a physician, meeting every week to review athlete health across disciplines. The results have compounded every year. This season marked the first time in the program’s history that no athlete sustained a bone stress injury, an outcome Edwards attributes directly to that coordinated care.

The model worked. The problem was access.

“In real life, it’s not something most people can do,” says Edwards. “There isn’t really a world where a recreational runner can go somewhere and have a dietician and a PT and an MD and get that education from all of them. Not everyone can come to Atlanta. And not everyone can afford to.”

She points to three barriers that define the recreational runner’s experience with injury: time, money and physical location. Most running specialists are out of network. Seeing more than one provider in a single week becomes expensive fast. And outside of a few major cities, finding a provider who truly understands running medicine can feel impossible.

What goes unspoken in most clinical settings, Edwards says, is what happens to a person while they’re still searching.

“When somebody has seen multiple providers and nobody has an answer, they start to question themselves,” she says. “They ask, am I crazy? Is this real? Some people get fearful and stop running entirely. Others push through and make it worse. Others end up dealing with depression or anxiety.”

Edwards knows this from more than clinical observation. When she was diagnosed with a cardiac condition that forced her off the road, she found herself on the receiving end of the same fragmented system. Test after test. No answers. She spiraled. That experience did not leave her practice. It shaped it.

RunSource launched with more than 40 vetted running medicine professionals contributing content across physical therapy, sports medicine, registered dietetics, certified strength coaching and sports psychology. Every piece is curated through what Edwards calls the expert filter, a vetting process that mirrors the same clinical rigor she applies at Precision Performance.

The app features two proprietary AI agents. Katherine walks users through an educational symptom checker that draws from the same protocols Edwards uses in her practice. Andrew answers general running questions using a curated knowledge base of peer-reviewed research and expert-produced content. Neither guesses. If either agent doesn’t know the answer, it says so. If Katherine flags signs of a bone stress injury, it tells the user to see a physician.

For injured runners looking for a place to start, RunSource covers:

“Much of what we do as clinicians is educate,” says Edwards. “Ninety percent of an appointment is the education and what you need to do to help yourself. That piece is what I built the app around.”

One philosophy sits at the center of all of it: she does not tell runners to stop running.

With limited exceptions, such as confirmed bone stress injuries, Edwards believes that pulling a runner entirely off the road does as much harm as it does good. A tendon injury, she explains, is not helped by rest alone. What it needs is appropriate loading, a modification in training volume and targeted eccentric work. Stopping affects the runner not just emotionally but physiologically, in ways that slow recovery rather than support it.

Edwards spent three years building the answer she once searched for herself. When her cardiac diagnosis forced her off the road and left her cycling through specialists with no explanation, she did not find coordinated care. She found the same fragmented system her patients describe every day.

RunSource is her response to that system.

“Every runner deserves access to the kind of care that elite athletes get,” says Edwards. “RunSource does not replace a provider when you need one. It tells you when you need one, what kind to find, and gives you expert guidance in the meantime.”

That is the model she helped build for the Atlanta Track Club Elite, distilled into an app and handed to every runner with a phone.

#8718. The Best Creatine Supplements for Men for Muscle Growth and Enhanced Recovery

We tried 43 creatine supplements and evaluated them for factors like taste, mixability, and dosage. Here are our top seven picks.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Creatine is a popular muscle-building supplement, and for good reason. It’s one of the most research-backed supplements for muscle growth and recovery. While some people associate creatine with weightlifters or bodybuilders, it’s a great supplement for anyone looking to build muscle, enhance their performance, and promote better recovery.

There are tons of creatine supplements on the market, including powders, pills, and gummies. These supplements use various forms of creatine (more on that later), and some contain other ingredients that aim to help you grow muscle, recover faster, or sharpen your focus in the gym.

On one hand, having such a wide variety of options can be empowering. On the other hand, it can be a challenge to figure out which is right for you.

To narrow down the field to only the best of the best, our expert product testers tried dozens of creatine supplements ranging from standard powders to convenient capsules to flavorful gummies. We looked for creatine supplements that taste good, mix well (when applicable), use quality ingredients, contain enough creatine per serving, and are affordable. Along the way, we spoke with certified personal trainers and nutritionists for guidance.

Below are our picks for the best creatine supplements for men. However, individuals of any gender can choose from this lineup with confidence.

Disclaimer: While this article is intended for educational and informational purposes, it should not be viewed as a substitute for medical advice. Furthermore, we intend the term “men” to include all men, including trans men. However, we understand most research on this topic has focused on cis men (men who are not trans). When we reference gender-based research and nutritional recommendations, we will clarify by saying “cis men.” We encourage trans and nonbinary people of all genders to consult with a trans-competent nutritionist regarding their supplements and training needs.

Transparent Labs Creatine HMB is our pick for the best creatine monohydrate because it contains 5 grams of it per serving, which is the researched-backed dose for improved athletic performance. “This dose is a great recommendation for the general population, but some sports nutrition recommendations recommend a dosage based on kilograms of body weight, so some individuals may require more than 5 grams to see a benefit,” says Anna Marie Clear, M.S., R.D., C.P.T.

This dietary supplement contains β-hydroxy β-methylbutyrate (HMB), which the body naturally produces when it breaks down the amino acid leucine. Although more studies are needed, some research suggests HMB promotes muscle growth. “Leucine is the primary amino acid that triggers muscle protein synthesis,” Clear explains.”HMB and leucine are very similar, but research shows HMB has no greater effect than leucine alone.”

Transparent Labs also includes BioPerine, a derivative of black pepper that studies show increases nutrient bioavailability. “Bioperine may help enhance absorption of some nutrients, but research is limited on its impact alongside HMB and creatine,” says Clear.

Earning a perfect formulation score of 5 out of 5 stars, Creatine HMB also received high marks from our testing team for taste. Although it fell shy of another 5-star rating, this supplement earned a solid score of 4 out of 5 in this all-important category.

Transparent Labs Creatine HMB comes in 13 flavors, including an unflavored version. This is a lot more flavor options than you’ll find in most creatine supplements and the most of any on our list.

Pete Nastasi, C.P.T., C.S.N.C., tried this supplement. “I’ve tried both the Blue Raspberry and Strawberry Lemonade flavors, which are sweetened with stevia extract, and both tasted great,” he says. “I love having a flavored creatine supplement in the morning before my morning workout.”

However, while Nastasi liked the flavor, other testers say this supplement has a slightly bitter taste, which they attribute to the BioPerine.

“I tried Black Cherry and I wasn’t a huge fan of the taste of this one—it tasted a bit watered down, even with the right amount of water,” our product tester noted. “Some people may prefer this though!”

While another tester also noted some tartness due to the BioPerine, she’s still optimistic about the Tropical Punch flavor.

“I bought this at the end of winter but I’m looking forward to drinking it in the summer because I find something refreshing about it that I think will be nice during the hotter months,” she explained.

We chose Sports Research Creatine Monohydrate as our top pick for athletes because it contains 5 grams of creatine per serving, which research shows is an optimal dose for muscle gain, muscle recovery, and overall improved athletic performance. For this reason, we rated the formulation a 5 out of 5.

This creatine is also a great choice for athletes because it’s Informed Sport Certified—this third party tests for purity and banned substances. So, if you’re planning on competing in any events, you can feel good knowing this product is certified banned substance-free.

Another benefit of this supplement is that it uses micronized creatine. Micronized creatine is ground into finer particles than non-micronized so it dissolves much more easily in water. However, according to Nastasi, “micronized creatine is a bit of a marketing gimmick—it isn’t digested any better than standard creatine monohydrate.”

Research supports Nastasi, as this 2022 study says there is “no evidence” that micronized creatine is more bioavailable than non-micronized creatine.

However, using micronized creatine does contribute to excellent solubility. Our tester showed no hesitation giving Sports Research Creatine Monohydrate a 5-star rating in this category.

“If you didn’t tell me there was creatine in this water I wouldn’t know—it’s truly tasteless and mixes easily,” our tester reported.

Unfortunately for your taste buds, this supplement only comes in an unflavored version. However, while some creatine powders can have a bitter aftertaste, this one doesn’t.

“It tastes just like water,” our tester noted. One thing to consider about this creatine supplement is that it only comes as a powder. If you prefer creatine capsules (or a flavored powder), you’ll want to look elsewhere.

If you don’t like measuring out and mixing powders, you’re in luck. Swoly Creatine Mono Gummies are ideal for athletes on the go who don’t want to carry around an additional shaker bottle for their creatine.

Although they only come in one flavor (Strawberry), Swoly knocked it out of the park from a taste perspective, earning a perfect score of 5 out of 5 from one of our most experienced product testers.

“These are dangerously delicious — like, need-to-make-sure-my-child-doesn’t-find-these-or-she-will-eat-them all kind of delicious,” our tester eloquently described. “They remind me of the BEST fruit snacks.”

Concerned about the texture? No need to worry about that, either. Our product tester also gave Swoly a 5-star rating for swallowability.

“Super easy and delicious. I’d eat these every day,” she noted.

As much as our tester enjoyed chowing down on these creatine gummies, be aware that one serving is five gummies, which can be a lot for some people. Plus, one serving only contains 4 grams of creatine monohydrate, which is a little shy of our preferred dosage of 5 grams. Our R.D. reviewer, Anna Marie Clear, notes that “larger individuals may need to take more of these gummies to get their research-backed dose of 0.1 grams of creatine per kilogram of body weight.”

If that’s you, you may want to opt for a different option, since taking more than five gummies could “lead to GI symptoms because of the added sugar and gums,” she says.

Unlike some other creatine supplements on this list, Swoly gummies contain more than a few added ingredients, including artificial ingredients. They also have 15 calories per serving and 2.5 grams of added sugar per serving from sucrose, dextrose, and maltodextrin.

As a result, we give the formulation 4 out of 5 stars since we prefer 5 grams of creatine monohydrate per serving and the added sugar may not align with some consumers’ dietary preferences.

Although Swoly says these gummies are third-party tested, there’s no information about through which organization. As a result, we could only give 3 out of 5 stars in this category.

If you’re looking for a budget-friendly creatine supplement, you can’t do much better than Nutricost. At just $0.20 per serving, this supplement is the cheapest on our list. But cheap doesn’t equate to low-quality—Nutricost creatine is third-party tested, which is something you typically only find in more expensive supplements.

“This company does not elaborate on its third-party testing,” Clear says. “It’s hard to determine the brand’s safety without a detailed explanation of its testing process.”

Although we docked a few points for the lack of transparency in third-party testing by giving 3 out of 5 stars, Nutricost earned a perfect formulation score.

“It’s recommended to take 3-5 grams of creatine daily to enhance athletic performance, and Nutricost provides 5 grams daily, ensuring your muscle cells remain saturated,” says registered dietitian Perry Nix.

Our product tester reported no adverse side effects when taking Nutricost. In fact, he was pleasantly surprised that he didn’t experience any bloating like he did with other creatine products.

Another benefit of this creatine supplement is that it comes in five flavor options, which is more than most brands offer for creatine supplements. Flavors include Blue Raspberry, Fruit Punch, Pineapple Mango, Watermelon, and Unflavored. However, these flavors are sweetened with sucralose, which research shows may cause gut issues in some people when consumed in high doses.

One of the few knocks against this budget-friendly creatine is its solubility; or potentially, the lack thereof. Our tester only gave it 3 out of 5 stars, noting that “it settles quite a bit.”

Amazon reviewers are pleased with this product, giving it 4.6/5 stars overall. Many praise its lack of additional ingredients and effective formula. “It has made a significant positive impact on my workout performance and recovery,” says Amazon reviewer Kurt. However, a few reviewers mention finding pieces of plastic in their containers, which is something to watch out for.

Some unflavored creatine tastes chalky and a little bitter (no bueno!). If you drink your creatine with water, a flavored option like Legion Recharge should suit your taste buds better. Legion offers this supplement in six flavors, which although not as vast as Transparent Labs’ variety, taste better, according to customers and our team of experts.

Our product tester tried the Strawberry Lemonade flavor, giving it a perfect 5-out-of-5 rating for taste.

“It’s pretty sweet but also tart. I really liked it” she noted.

Many customers on Amazon attest to how good Legion’s flavors are, with a few noting that Strawberry Lemonade and Fruit Punch are particularly good. However, some reviewers mention the Unflavored version has an unpleasant, bitter flavor.

One thing you won’t have to worry about with Recharge is solubility. Our tester reported the power dissolved perfectly with no clumps or sediment at the bottom of her shaker cup, leading to another 5-out-of-5 rating.

Similarly, we’re also big fans of the formulation. Legion Recharge has a research-backed dose of 5g of creatine per serving. The creatine is micronized, which means it’s been processed to be finer. Legion says this makes it easier to blend and less likely to cause an upset stomach. However, our R.D. reviewer Anna Marie Clear notes, “While micronized creatine monohydrate is processed to be finer, the research does not support the micronized version to be more bioavailable.”

Legion Recharge also contains 2.1 grams of L-carnitine in each serving, which helps the body convert fat into energy, and 10.5 grams of corosolic acid, which research shows helps regulate blood sugar.

Unfortunately for budget-conscious shoppers, Recharge is one of the more expensive options on this list, checking in at $1.33 per serving. As a result, we could only give it 1.5 out of 5 stars for price. So, if you’re on a tight budget, you may want to go with something like Nutricost.

Related Post: The Best Non-Stim Pre-Workouts

If you don’t like the taste of creatine powder or find it a pain to mix, Optimum Nutrition Micronized Creatine Capsules are a convenient and tasteless alternative. Plus, a bottle of these capsules will take up less room in your gym bag than a tub of creatine powder.

Optimum Nutrition offers three sizes: 100 capsules for $30 ($0.60/serving), 200 capsules for $50 ($0.50/serving), or 300 capsules for $69 ($0.46/serving). Optimum Nutrition recommends you take two capsules twice daily since one serving (two capsules) only contains 2.5 grams of creatine.

That may not be a deterrent for some folks, but our team docked a few points off the formulation, giving Optimum Nutrition 3 out of 5 stars in this key category.

“You can always double the intake, but four pills is a lot and makes the serving size much more expensive,” our product tester noted.

Furthermore, our R.D. reviewer Anna Marie Clear notes: “A larger athlete (ie. 100 kilograms) would need to take eight capsules (10 grams of creatine) in order to meet the 1 gram per kilogram of body weight recommendation.” So if you’re a bigger person, you may want to opt for a powder that’s easier to take more of.

These capsules have a simple ingredient list: creatine monohydrate, gelatin, and magnesium stearate. Magnesium stearate and gelatin form the capsule. Gelatin is an animal product, so these supplements are not vegan.

As for how easy they go down? Our product tester rated the swallowability 5 out of 5 stars.

“They are tasteless aside from a slight gelatin flavor,” he says. “And the pills are a bit large—about 1 inch long—but I didn’t have trouble swallowing them.”

If you’re trying to achieve some gnarly gains, you can’t go wrong with an affordably priced supplement made with the most widely used brand of creatine. Experts consider CreaPure®, a branded form of creatine monohydrate, the gold standard for purity and effectiveness. Nastasi agrees: “It’s manufactured in Germany and is super pure, so from a purity perspective it’s no. 1.”

Gnarly is the only supplement on our list with this form of creatine. Each serving contains 5 grams of 100% CreaPure® creatine monohydrate, putting it ahead of the class and leading to a formulation score of 5 out of 5 stars. This research-backed dose can help support your physique-building efforts, as combining creatine supplementation with adequate resistance training is shown to be an effective muscle growth strategy.

In addition, Gnarly Creatine is NSF Certified for Sport and NSF Content Certified. This means it’s third-party certified to be pure and free from banned substances. This is great news for athletes who compete in drug-tested athletic competitions, since testing positive for banned substances, even if they’re consumed by accident, can lead to disqualification. So, if you’re an aspiring bodybuilder looking to pack on as much muscle as possible, you don’t have to worry about any issues with Gnarly.

“NSF Certified for Sport also indicates this supplement has undergone label claim testing (so the label is accurate) and contaminant testing for heavy metals, microbes, and pesticides,” says Clear. “This may be the most pure option on this list,” she adds.

While Gnarly earned a perfect third-party testing rating, it didn’t live up to our standards for solubility, leading to a disappointing score of 3 out of 5 stars.

“It doesn’t mix very well and settles quite a bit,” our product tester noted. “I usually end up stirring it several times while I take it.”Many Amazon reviews echo similar sentiments, so if you’re searching for a smooth sipping experience, consider an alternative like Sports Research.

Our team tested dozens of other creatines to come up with this list, with many of us relying on some form of this popular supplement for years. However, not every creatine product could make our list, so here are some honorable mentions that didn’t quite make the cut:

Our team has tried more than 43 creatine supplements in total, with more added on the regular. We evaluate each supplement for the following factors:

There are a few key factors you’ll want to consider when choosing a creatine supplement.

Research shows the most efficacious dose of creatine is between 3 and 5 grams for most individuals. Look for supplements with servings within this range if you’re looking for maximum benefits, including increased muscle mass, faster recovery, and improved exercise capacity. Remember, larger individuals may require more creatine for maximum benefits—0.1 grams per kilogram of body weight is the research-backed recommendation.

Some supplements have additional ingredients to bolster the product’s effectiveness. Transparent Labs, for example, includes HMB, which some research shows promotes muscle growth, though more research is needed. Legion includes L-carnitine, which research shows helps metabolize fat into energy. Consider your goals and whether or not you want a pure creatine supplement or one with other athletic performance-enhancing ingredients.

“I highly recommend collaborating with a sports dietitian to find the most optimal supplement for you based on your personal health, athletic, or physique goals and to ensure you are consuming an appropriate dosage from a safe and high-quality supplement,” says Anna Marie Clear, our expert reviewer and R.D.

Some creatine supplements use artificial ingredients and fillers to help improve taste and mixability. While many of the products on our list contain creatine as their sole ingredient, some, like Swoly gummies, use some artificial ingredients. Consider whether or not it’s important for your supplement to be completely pure.

Third-party testing is the best way to ensure that your supplement’s ingredients are pure and match what’s on the label. Supplements are not regulated by the FDA, so third-party testing gives consumers confidence in their products.

“It is also especially important to consider third-party testing for sport certifications from either Informed Sport or NSF Certified for Sport if you are a collegiate or professional athlete or if you are looking to compete in a weightlifting, bodybuilding, or other fitness competition to ensure you are consuming supplements free from banned substances,” says Clear.

Creatine phosphate (CrP) is a compound made of three amino acids: arginine, glycine, and methionine. The body produces creatine naturally in the liver, kidneys, and pancreas, with about 95% of it found in skeletal muscle. “Through diet, creatine is found primarily in red meat and seafood, however, to get an extra creatine boost, a creatine powder or pill supplement can help,” says personal trainer and strength coach Will Duru.

Creatine supplies energy to muscles through the phosphocreatine system. “Creatine helps in the production of ATP (adenosine triphosphate)—the compound that provides energy to bodily processes such as muscle contraction,” nutritionist Rob Hobson says. “Creatine can help with the production of ATP during maximum-effort exercises, such as sprints or intense muscular effort lasting between five and 10 seconds. It can also help recovery between exercise bouts.”

Hobson says creatine can improve performance in sports involving repeated sprints, such as rugby or football, and high-intensity bursts, like track or swim sprints. “Creatine can also help you train harder through being able to do more work over a series of training sets,” he adds.

As a certified personal trainer, former rugby player, and longtime lifter, I can attest to the impact that creatine has on both performance and recovery. It’s been a staple in my supplement stack for years, and despite myths about unwanted weight gain and water retention, I’ve never experienced those side effects.

As the most-researched supplement on the market, creatine has long been utilized by everyone from professional athletes to strength training enthusiasts to casual lifters. Let’s explore some of the positive potential effects of creatine supplementation:

“Research shows creatine supplementation helps muscle performance throughout a number of activities including soccer training, weight training, plyometric training, and even canoe training,” says Duru. Interestingly, this study also showed that muscle power output and muscle strength still increased with creatine supplementation, even when research subjects didn’t do any exercise. This is in comparison to subjects who took a placebo supplement.

“There are lots of studies showing how creatine supplementation can improve strength, power, and high-intensity exercise performance. This is due to the role it plays in energy production and its ability to increase ATP availability during short bursts of intense activity,” says nutritionist Rob Hobson.

Want to build muscle? Creatine could be your go-to. “Creatine supplementation is often used to increase muscle mass. It can draw more water into your muscle cells, creating a cell volumization effect that may promote muscle growth,” says Hobson. “Additionally, creatine can enhance the effects of resistance training by increasing total muscle mass and strength gains.”

According to a 2023 meta-analysis on the effects of creatine supplementation combined with resistance training, this protocol can promote “a small increase in the direct measures of skeletal muscle hypertrophy in both the upper and lower body.”

Duru says for maximum muscle-building results, creatine loading can help. “The first time you take creatine, take around 20 to 25 grams of creatine every day for up to a week, broken up into 5-gram servings across the day. Then drop to the recommended 3 to 5 grams the day after this.”

Clear adds: “If you are looking to initiate creatine supplementation with a loading dose of 20 grams per day, I recommend breaking this large dosage into smaller servings throughout the day to minimize gastrointestinal distress (i.e., diarrhea).”

Recovery is key when training. Not only does it help you avoid injury, but a speedier recovery means we can get back to exercise quicker. Research shows creatine supplementation may reduce recovery time between spurts of intense exercise by reducing muscle damage.

Although supplementing with creatine does not entirely prevent muscle damage, studies show creatine reduces the immediate muscle damage that occurs after resistance training.

Studies show creatine can benefit brain function. “Creatine supplementation may have a beneficial effect on brain function, as the brain requires a significant amount of ATP for normal operation. It may be particularly beneficial in tasks requiring speed and quick thinking,” says Hobson.

Creatine supplementation is also important for overall health and wellness as you age. According to a 2021 study led by renowned creatine researcher Dr. Darren Candow, one year of creatine supplementation and resistance training had favorable effects on bone area and muscle density in older adults. This included both male and female participants, suggesting no differences between sex when it comes to creatine’s impact.

Not all creatine is created equal. In fact, there are multiple forms. Here’s a brief overview of the different types of creatine so you understand what to look for and what might suit you best.

Creatine monohydrate consists of creatine paired with a water molecule. As nutritionist Rob Hobson notes, this is the most research-backed form of creatine, and it’s typically the primary form used in most of the best-selling supplements in this category.

“Micronized creatine is processed to create smaller particles than the standard creatine powder,” Hobson says. “The intention of micronized creatine is to improve its solubility and absorption in the body so creatine is then used up by muscles more quickly.”

In this form, creatine is bound to ester salts, which some studies show makes the creatine more easily absorbed within the body. However, research shows creatine ethyl ester is not as effective as monohydrate.

Creatine nitrate is derived from the same molecule as creatine monohydrate but with a nitrate added. Some studies suggest creatine nitrate is more bioavailable than monohydrate, but results are mixed and more research is needed. Currently, creatine nitrate is only approved by the FDA at a daily dose of 750 milligrams per day.

This type of creatine is normally manufactured with added alkaline, so it has a higher pH than regular creatine monohydrate. However, research shows there is little difference between buffered creatine and creatine monohydrate when it comes to training gains.

A creatine loading phase involves taking a higher dose of creatine, typically between 20 and 25 grams, for up to a week, according to Duru. He recommends reducing to a dose of 3 to 5 grams a day after a week.

“A lot of people do a creatine loading phase to fully saturate the muscles when they first start taking creatine, and this can potentially speed up the benefits by a few days,” says Pete Nastasi, CPT, CSNC. “But if you take more than two to three days off from creatine, it’s likely that your creatine stores will go back down to baseline and you might want to do another loading phase,” he says. “That’s why I suggest people take it every day.”

Studies show creatine loading phases (e.g. 20 grams per day for five to seven days) can help increase muscle creatine storage by 10 to 30 percent. However, creatine loading phases aren’t necessary. Studies show that long term, you can achieve the same effects without a loading phase. But if it’s speed you’re after, loading phases are a safe and effective way to quickly improve gains.

Studies show creatine supplementation is safe in both the short and long term for healthy individuals. Healthy people can safely take up to 30 grams per day for up to five years. However, as we’ll explain below, those with certain health conditions should avoid creatine supplements.

“Since creatine is a safe supplement, there aren’t many precautions to take beyond sticking to the recommended dosage,” says nutritionist Rob Hobson. “Like all supplements, figure out if it is really necessary to suit your performance goals, as there is little point in taking it if it is not. If you are training for a marathon then it’s not really going to be of use to you but if you are looking to build more muscle and become stronger, then it’s a good choice.”

Creatine works for most people, but those with certain pre-existing health conditions should avoid it. “Anyone with pre-existing kidney or liver conditions or impaired function should avoid creatine,” says Hobson. Experts say creatine supplements may prevent those with kidney or liver problems from producing their own creatine. “Anyone taking medications affecting kidney function should avoid creatine or speak to their GP first. This might include blood pressure medication or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs on a regular basis,” Hobson adds.

Hobson also advises against creatine supplementation for those younger than 18. “With adolescents, while the research suggests it may be okay for this age group, I avoid recommending it as the long-term effects are not fully understood yet,” he says.

While myths exist about water retention, cramping, and even its legality, creatine is one of the most researched-backed supplements. If you’re a dedicated lifter looking to enhance your muscle gains, improve your performance in activities requiring short bursts of energy, or hasten your recovery, you shouldn’t hesitate to add one of the options from our list to your stack.

All you have to decide is whether you prefer a powder, pill, or gummy and you’ll be well on your way to unlocking the benefits of this uber-popular supplement.

Micronized creatine is processed to create smaller particles than the standard creatine powder. “Research shows micronized creatine monohydrate is not any more bioavailable than creatine monohydrate itself,” says R.D. Anna Marie Clear.

According to nutritionist Rob Hobson, most people take creatine after working out. “Research shows taking creatine after your workout may be marginally more beneficial given the increased uptake by muscles during this period, as exercise increases blood flow to muscle tissue,” he says.Hobson recommends taking creatine with a meal or a drink containing carbohydrates. “The effects of insulin help transport creatine into muscle cells,” he says.

In short, no. According to the International Society of Sports Nutrition, “There is no scientific evidence that the short- or long-term use of creatine monohydrate has any detrimental effects on otherwise healthy individuals.”

Research shows the best dose is from 3 to 5 grams per day for most individuals. However, as R.D. Anna Marie Clear notes, the research-backed dose of 0.1 grams of creatine per kilogram of body weight means some larger individuals will need more than 5 grams per day to see optimal results.

Creatine may help increase your lean skeletal muscle mass, which can, in turn, increase your overall body weight. This overall increase in lean body mass will likely improve your body composition, as creatine supplementation does not impact your fat mass. “Good quality randomized controlled trials (one week to two years in duration) show creatine supplementation does not increase fat mass. Acute creatine supplementation (seven days) had no effect on fat mass in young and older adults; however, fat-free mass increased.”

Stephen is an ISSA-certified personal trainer and nutritionist with an immense passion for health and fitness. A two-time University of Florida graduate and longtime rugby player, he brings more than a decade of strength training experience, plus a diverse writing and editing background. When he’s not creating content or hitting the gym, he enjoys traveling, cooking, and attending music festivals around the world.

The 2026 Amateur Olympia brought international bodybuilding talent to Las Vegas, where competitors battled for overall titles and the opportunity to earn IFBB Pro League status during Olympia Weekend.

The next generation of professional bodybuilding talent took center stage September 22–23 at the 2026 Amateur Olympia Las Vegas. Held at the Pearl Theater inside the Palms Casino Resort during Joe Weider’s Olympia Fitness & Performance Weekend, the competition brought together amateur athletes from around the world, all competing for championship titles and the opportunity to earn an IFBB Pro League card.

As one of the premier amateur bodybuilding competitions associated with Olympia Weekend, the Amateur Olympia provides aspiring professionals with an opportunity to compete on an international stage while taking an important step toward the professional ranks.

This year’s competition featured standout performances across men’s and women’s divisions, including Men’s Bodybuilding, Classic Physique, Men’s Physique, Women’s Bodybuilding, Women’s Physique, Figure, Bikini, Wellness, and Fit Model.

For the athletes who earned overall victories, the weekend represented more than a championship. It marked the beginning of a new chapter in their competitive bodybuilding careers.

One of the weekend’s standout performances came from Lithuania’s Albertas Krinickis, who captured the Men’s Bodybuilding overall championship. At just 20 years old, Krinickis demonstrated impressive muscular development and conditioning in the super heavyweight division, ultimately securing his IFBB Pro League card.

Having previously competed in Classic Physique, his transition to Men’s Bodybuilding and success at the Amateur Olympia made his victory particularly noteworthy.

In an Instagram post following the competition, Krinickis reflected on just how much his physique had changed over the previous year.

“From 12th place in Classic Physique to an Open Bodybuilding Overall Champion!” he wrote, highlighting the progress he had made in a relatively short period.

The transformation was also reflected in his competition weight. During a post-show interview, Krinickis discussed moving from approximately 200 pounds at his previous competition to 240 pounds onstage in Las Vegas.

“Last year I competed at around 200 pounds, while for the Amateur Olympia I stepped onstage at 240 pounds. The work done on mass and structure paid off every bit of effort,” Krinickis said in comments translated from the post-show interview.

The victory established Krinickis as one of the young names to watch as he begins his professional bodybuilding career.

Germany’s Rene Hildebrand claimed the Men’s Classic Physique overall title, while Peru’s Edward Alonso Guillen Alva secured the Men’s Physique overall championship. Both athletes earned professional status through their respective victories.

The men’s division highlighted the international depth of amateur bodybuilding, with competitors representing different countries and bringing a range of physiques and competitive backgrounds to the Olympia stage.

The women’s divisions delivered an equally competitive showcase, with athletes earning championship honors across several categories.

Haley May of the United States captured the Women’s Bodybuilding overall title, while Australia’s Nicole Beeforth won the Women’s Physique overall championship and earned her IFBB Pro League card.

Beeforth’s victory was particularly significant for Australian bodybuilding. According to the GMV International Museum of Bodybuilding, she became the first Australian woman to earn an IFBB Pro League card at the Las Vegas Amateur Olympia.

In Figure, Kerri Ferns of the United States claimed the overall victory. Nicole Grumblatt took top honors in Bikini, while Ana Carolina De La Mora won the Wellness overall championship.

Alissa Christine rounded out the women’s overall champions by capturing the Fit Model title.

The variety of women’s divisions reflects the continued growth of competitive bodybuilding and physique sports, providing athletes with different competitive pathways based on muscular development, conditioning, symmetry, and presentation.

The Amateur Olympia serves an important role in the bodybuilding industry by providing athletes with a pathway toward professional competition.

Earning an IFBB Pro League card is a significant milestone for amateur competitors. It gives qualified athletes the opportunity to enter professional-level contests and begin pursuing the next stage of their careers.

For many competitors, the opportunity to earn professional status during Olympia Weekend makes the accomplishment particularly meaningful. The event connects emerging bodybuilding talent with the sport’s most established athletes, industry professionals, and fans.

The international field also reinforces bodybuilding’s continued global growth. Athletes travel to Las Vegas from across the world to compete, bringing different training backgrounds and competitive experiences to one of the sport’s most recognized stages.

According to Cayden Riley, Producer of Amateur Olympia Las Vegas, the quality of competition and the athlete experience remain central to the event’s continued development.

“Every year, the level of competition continues to rise. We have incredible athletes coming from around the world, and the energy they bring to the Amateur Olympia is something special. Jake Wood and Dan Solomon have always emphasized putting the athletes first, and their leadership continues to inspire us to create an unforgettable experience for every competitor who steps on the Olympia stage,” Riley said.

Riley also emphasized the significance of helping athletes reach the professional level.

“Our goal is to give these athletes an unforgettable experience and a stage worthy of the Olympia name. Seeing them earn their IFBB Pro cards and realize their dreams is what makes this event so rewarding,” he added.

For the overall champions of the 2026 Amateur Olympia Las Vegas, earning professional status marks the beginning of a new competitive opportunity.

The transition from amateur to professional bodybuilding brings a different level of competition, with athletes facing established IFBB professionals and working toward opportunities to qualify for major professional events.

While each athlete’s competitive path will be different, the Amateur Olympia provides a platform for emerging talent to introduce themselves to the broader bodybuilding community.

The 2026 competition once again demonstrated the depth of international bodybuilding talent and the importance of developing opportunities for athletes working toward professional status.

For these newly crowned champions, Las Vegas was more than the site of a major amateur competition. It was the place where their professional bodybuilding journeys began.

Garmin GPS head units are one of the smartest upgrades you can make to your road, gravel, mountain, or electric bike, and a much safer alternative than strapping your phone to the bars to see your route. Cycling computers also capture, process, and display data from accessories like heart rate monitors, power meters, and even electronic shifting to help you ride better, train smarter, and stay connected. And because Garmin lets you customize nearly everything—from data fields to navigation screens—you can tailor exactly what shows up.

Buying Tip: Buying previous-generation cycling computers is a great way to save money. Older models usually have almost the same performance at a big discount. Cyclists often even prefer the old models if they’re lighterweight or have better battery life.

Cycling radar is one of the most important pieces of bicycle technology released in the last decade. On-bike radar systems mount to the rear of your bike and feature an integrated taillight. Paired with a cycling computer or smartwatch, they notify you about vehicles approaching from behind so you can move out of the way. They are a must-have item for road and gravel riders.

Not sure which radar you need? Check out my comparison below.

Buying Tip: Garmin is a pioneer in cycling radar tech and makes the most reliable, consistent systems. The Varia RTL515 is our benchmark and best-value pick, while the RearVue 820 is newer and more powerful; it’s our choice for best performance. The RCT715 is the 515 with an integrated rear-facing camera.

While dedicated cycling computers are the go-to choice for road, gravel, and data-heavy training, many riders prefer Garmin’s smartwatches because they keep everything in one place, especially when they track more than bike rides—anyone who mixes riding with running, hiking, paddling, strength training, or even walking the dog. Garmin watches have powerful GPS, workout metrics, and daily health data in a streamlined device that’s always with you (and they even tell time).

Buying Tip: Mountain bikers often appreciate the simplicity and safety of recording their rides from the wrist rather than risking a pricey head unit in a crash. Triathletes, duathletes, and cyclocross racers love the seamless transitions a watch allows. There’s no need to swap devices or merge files after an event.

Most riders know Garmin from its computers, smartwatches, and cycling radar. But Garmin also owns the indoor trainer brand Tacx. Its smart trainers and indoor bikes are highly regarded for their excellent performance, integration, and useful features. One cool feature we love—especially if you live somewhere prone to winter power outages—is that the Neo 2T generates its own resistance electromagnetically. That means you don’t have to scrap your workout plans just because the lights go out.

Power pedals, like Garmin’s Rally series, are easier to install than crank-based power meter options. Plus, you can swap power pedals easily between bikes. This not only saves cost, but it also gives you consistent data from bike to bike.

Buying Tip: Garmin offers a handy option to buy its power meter in a package including two pedal styles (road and mountain bike/gravel) with swappable spindles. This way you can measure power across riding disciplines.

#8713. Our Editors Tested the Zwift Ride Against Pricier Indoor Bikes. Now It’s $999 for Black Friday

Save on the Zwift Ride, Wahoo Kickr Core 2, and Cog & Click upgrades for indoor miles this winter.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Zwift’s Black Friday deals are here, and they’re the best discounts we’ve seen all year on the Zwift Ride Bike and Wahoo Kickr Core 2 trainer. The end of November usually means two things for cyclists: Riding the indoor trainer and scoring deals on cycling gear. This year, Zwift combines them for big savings on Bicycling’s two best-tested trainers.

The Ride is an indoor training bike that integrates seamlessly with Zwift’s popular virtual cycling platform—it’s a bicycle and trainer in one; you don’t even need to attach your outdoor bike. But if you want to ride your own bicycle in Watopia or train inside this winter, Zwift also has a great deal on our top-rated smart trainer, the Wahoo Kickr Core 2.

Training bikes are quickly gaining popularity among indoor riders. These purpose-built units integrate a bike and trainer for quick setup, easy use, and improved durability. With a training bike, you no longer have to fumble to get your bike on the trainer on a rainy day, swap bikes when a family member wants to ride Zwift, or prematurely wear out components on your pricey road, gravel, or mountain bike.

Until Zwift introduced its Ride bike, price has been the big downside to training bikes. Popular models are $2,500 to $4,000; the Ride’s $1,300 everyday price cuts that cost in half—Zwift’s Black Friday deal trims it to only $999. That’s a complete, Zwift-ready indoor bike for less than the price of some direct drive trainers.

How does Zwift do it? Instead of overthinking things, Zwift combines the excellent Wahoo Kickr Core 2 smart trainer with a stripped-down bicycle frame. But instead of building up this frame with pricey components that wear out quickly, it uses a robust singlespeed drivetrain and shift levers with built-in controls for use on the Zwift platform.

The Ride also features easily adjustable seat height, handlebar height, and bar reach. If you want to use your own saddle or a different bar, the Ride uses standard sizing for easy swaps. Zwift also recently updated Ride with crank length options and more fore-aft saddle adjustment. This means almost anyone can fit on the bike, and it makes it easy to share the Ride with multiple riders in your home.

Seeing the price, it’s easy to assume the Zwift Ride’s low price means a lower-quality experience. However, in head-to-head testing against much more expensive training bikes, the Ride walked away as our editors’ clear pick for most indoor cyclists.

Wahoo’s best-priced indoor trainer is actually the brand’s best overall. The Kickr Core 2 packs all of the accuracy, simplicity, and power of the range-topping Kickr smart trainer into a better-priced package. As Test Editor Dan Chabanov stated in his full-length review, “The Core 2 delivers nearly all of the real-world experience of Wahoo’s flagship trainer at a price that’s roughly 50 percent lower.” And that’s saying a lot: Chabanov is a former elite cyclocross and road racer, and still competes at a high level in Zwift’s racing leagues.

The Kickr Core 2 is a great deal at its everyday price of $550, and at $400 it’s a steal! The Core 2 features a smooth 11.9-pound flywheel with up to 1,800 watts max resistance, 16-percent gradient simulation, and quick connections via Bluetooth and ANT+ protocols. For updates and smooth data connection, Wahoo added WiFi connectivity to the Core trainer. It also features Zwift Race Mode for better connection and data transfer when racing online.

The 30-pound Kickr Core 2 fits bikes with 130mm and 135mm quick release dropouts or thru-axle-equipped bikes with 142mm or 148mm dropout spacing. The Core 2 has more stable legs than the original model; they work well for all but elite-level sprint efforts. Compared to the top-tier Kickr, the Core 2’s only downsides are its lack of a carrying handle and that it doesn’t fold as small for storage.

This version of the Kickr Core 2 also includes Zwift’s Cog and Click system. The singlespeed Cog replaces a traditional cassette and works with 8- to 13-speed drivetrains. This means you can use most bikes on the Core 2 without worrying about cassette compatibility—it’s great for riders who train indoors on multiple bikes (for example, a gravel bike one day and a road bike another ride) or for households with more than one user.

The Click is two small video game-style controllers you mount to your bar to virtually shift your bike in Zwift. The buttons can also award kudos, use power-ups, and scroll menus inside Zwift’s Watopia universe.

Already have a trainer you like? With the Cog and Click, you never need to worry about your bike’s cassette range or compatibility. You can still get in on the big Zwift discounts. Zwift’s Cog replaces your cassette on most direct-drive trainers (see list here) and installs in only a few minutes. Then, use the Click controllers to shift gears, use power-ups, give kudos, and operate menus in Zwift. It’s the perfect upgrade for any indoor rider.
